why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Missing-annotation effects have been examined for frequent-class benchmarks, but a quantified audit of tail-class false-positive validity under federated protocols may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample rare-class false positives across several methods, obtain careful human verdicts with clear instance-definition guidelines, and recompute evaluation metrics with audited corrections.
main_risk: Human auditors face the same ambiguity that produced sparse annotation, so audit instructions and inter-auditor agreement need to be reported alongside conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Evaluation-time penalties are assumed to reflect genuine model errors, with the federated protocol treated as an adequate approximation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The rarer the class, the less exhaustive its annotation coverage, and simultaneously the more each false positive costs in AP, an interaction that concentrates measurement error exactly on the tail.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Audit one hundred sampled tail-class false positives from one strong public detector and report the fraction judged to be real objects.

one_line_idea: Web pretraining displaces rather than solves the long tail: per-class gains from vision-language pretraining track web caption frequency, leaving web-rare classes as badly off as before.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language pretrained detectors report improved performance on benchmark-rare classes, and benchmark rarity is measured by annotation counts in the detection dataset, not by concept frequency on the web.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The improvement on benchmark-rare classes is concentrated in classes that are rare in the benchmark but common in web captions, so when classes are re-stratified by web frequency, the tail problem reappears essentially unchanged, relocated to web-rare concepts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Regressing per-class gains of vision-language-pretrained detectors over supervised baselines on estimated web caption frequency will show a strong positive relationship, and the web-rare stratum will show gains near zero.
why_important: Claims that web-scale pretraining solves long-tail detection guide data strategy; if the tail merely moved, applications with genuinely rare concepts, defects, species, and specialized equipment, gain nothing from the trend.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frequency analyses of pretraining benefits exist for classification, but a re-stratification of detection long-tail progress by web-concept frequency may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate web caption frequencies for benchmark classes, compute per-class deltas between vision-language and supervised detectors, and compare gain distributions across benchmark-frequency versus web-frequency stratifications.
main_risk: Frequency estimation error and class-name ambiguity could weaken the regression, requiring multiple estimation methods for robustness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Vision-language pretraining is presented as the practical answer to long-tail detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pretraining transfers knowledge proportional to concept exposure, so it can only convert web-common benchmark-rare classes into easy ones while leaving universally rare concepts untouched.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Sort benchmark classes by a quick web-frequency proxy, compare per-class gains of one vision-language detector over one supervised baseline across strata, in a single analysis pass.

one_line_idea: Few-shot detection evaluation measures support-set luck: variance across support samples exceeds method gaps, and single-support reporting has produced unstable conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Few-shot detection methods are evaluated by adapting to a small support set of novel-class examples, and the specific support instances are often fixed by convention or sampled once.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Novel-class AP varies so strongly across equally valid support sets that the between-method variance is smaller than the within-method support variance, so method rankings from single-support evaluation frequently invert under resampling.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating several public few-shot detectors across many resampled support sets will show wide per-method AP distributions with heavy overlap, and the probability that the single-support ranking matches the mean-performance ranking will be well below 1.
why_important: If support luck dominates, few-shot detection progress claims need episodic evaluation as a reporting standard, and practical few-shot deployment needs support-selection guidance more than new adaptation methods.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Episodic protocols exist in few-shot classification, but a quantified support-variance-versus-method-variance decomposition for few-shot detection benchmarks may be underdocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resample many support sets per configuration, adapt each public method on each, and run a variance decomposition of novel-class AP into method, support, and interaction components.
main_risk: Computational cost of many adaptation runs is high for slow methods, potentially limiting the method pool.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported few-shot detection gaps are read as stable properties of methods rather than of the sampled supports.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With a handful of support instances, the information content of the support sample varies enormously, and adaptation quality is bounded by what the specific examples happen to show.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Rerun one public few-shot detector across ten support resamples for one benchmark configuration and plot the AP spread in a day.

one_line_idea: Long-tail methods overfit the benchmark's frequency histogram: retesting under resampled tail shapes reveals that gains are tied to one particular class-frequency profile.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Long-tail detection methods introduce hyperparameters and design choices tuned on a benchmark whose class-frequency histogram is one fixed sample of possible real-world imbalance profiles.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The gains of published long-tail methods are substantially specific to the tuned frequency profile, so re-creating the benchmark with a different tail shape by subsampling annotations reorders methods and shrinks average gains, revealing profile overfitting rather than general imbalance robustness.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training and evaluating a fixed method pool across several synthetically reshaped frequency profiles of the same underlying data will produce method rankings with low stability across profiles, while a plain baseline plus calibration remains comparatively stable.
why_important: Real deployments face arbitrary and shifting imbalance profiles, so methods that only work on one histogram provide false comfort, and benchmark culture should include profile-robustness as a criterion.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frequency-profile robustness as an explicit evaluation dimension for long-tail detection methods appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct multiple frequency-reshaped variants of one dataset by annotation subsampling, train representative methods on each, and quantify gain stability and rank stability across variants.
main_risk: Subsampling changes total data volume alongside profile shape, so volume-matched controls are needed to isolate the profile effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A method that improves tail AP on the standard benchmark is assumed to handle class imbalance in general.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Many long-tail mechanisms encode the training histogram explicitly or through tuned constants, making them estimators of one distribution rather than robust procedures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Retrain one prominent long-tail method on one reshaped profile of its benchmark and check whether its headline gain over the baseline survives.

one_line_idea: Tail classes are recognized by their habitats: rare-class detection succeeds mainly in stereotyped contexts, and out-of-context rare instances fail at much higher rates than out-of-context common ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Rare classes have few training instances, which tend to come from a narrow set of scenes, so context and category are more tightly coupled in the tail than in the head of the distribution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detectors learn tail classes largely as context-conditioned hypotheses, so the context dependence of detection, measured as the performance drop for out-of-context instances, increases systematically as training frequency decreases, making tail AP a measure of habitat recognition.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring per-class context dependence via context-swap composites or context-stratified evaluation will show the dependence anticorrelated with class training frequency across the vocabulary of a long-tail benchmark.
why_important: Rare things in unexpected places are the paradigmatic hard case of open-world perception, and if tail detection is habitat-bound, current long-tail metrics overstate readiness for exactly those cases.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context bias is studied in general, but its quantitative scaling with class frequency across a long-tail vocabulary may be uncharted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build context-swap or context-masking evaluations covering classes across the frequency spectrum, evaluate public long-tail detectors, and fit the relationship between context dependence and training frequency.
main_risk: Constructing fair out-of-context tests for hundreds of classes is laborious, suggesting automation via segmentation-based transplantation with artifact controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Tail-class AP improvements are interpreted as the model having learned the appearance of rare categories.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With few examples, the statistically efficient shortcut is to bind the category to its recurring scene signature rather than to its intrinsic appearance, and training rewards this shortcut.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Transplant a handful of rare-class instances into neutral scenes, run one detector, and compare recall against in-context instances of the same objects.

one_line_idea: Most tail-class failure is naming, not missing: hierarchical evaluation that credits superclass-correct detections reveals the long-tail gap is largely a fine-grained labeling gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard long-tail evaluation scores a detection as wrong when the predicted label differs from the annotated leaf category, even if the prediction is the correct superclass or a sibling category, and tail categories are often fine-grained variants of common concepts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large share of tail-class errors are detections with correct localization and superclass but wrong leaf label, so hierarchy-aware scoring shrinks the head-tail gap substantially and reorders long-tail methods by revealing which improve perception versus which improve fine-grained naming.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-scoring public long-tail detector predictions with superclass credit will close a substantial fraction of the head-tail AP gap, and the closure fraction will differ across methods enough to change rankings.
why_important: The remedy differs by diagnosis, missing objects call for detection improvements while misnaming calls for fine-grained discrimination or naming interfaces, and current metrics cannot distinguish the two.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hierarchical metrics exist for classification, but a decomposition of the detection long-tail gap into miss versus misname components with method-level consequences may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Map a long-tail vocabulary onto a hierarchy, re-score cached predictions of several methods under leaf-strict and superclass-credit metrics, and compare gap sizes and method orderings.
main_risk: Hierarchy construction choices affect results, so multiple independent hierarchies should be tested for conclusion stability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The head-tail AP gap is read as rare objects going undetected.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectness generalizes across related categories, so a detector often finds the rare object but loses the label lottery among fine-grained siblings, a completely different failure than blindness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one method on one benchmark, count how many tail-class misses correspond to overlapping detections labeled with a sibling or parent category, a cached-prediction analysis doable in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Copy-paste augmentation teaches paste detection: rare-class gains from copy-paste partly reflect boundary and compositing cues, and artifact-free insertion tests would show smaller true gains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Copy-paste augmentation, inserting segmented objects into new images, is a standard technique for boosting rare-class detection, and compositing leaves low-level traces such as boundary discontinuities and lighting mismatch.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained with copy-paste partially learn to associate the target classes with compositing artifacts, so their measured rare-class improvement is inflated relative to their improvement on naturally photographed rare instances, and the inflation grows with how artifact-prone the augmentation pipeline is.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing rare-class gains on naturally photographed test instances against gains on composited test instances will show systematically larger gains on composited ones, and models will fire more readily on artifact-bearing pasted objects than on seamless insertions of the same objects.
why_important: If augmentation gains are partly artifact recognition, the field overestimates how much synthetic data mixing helps the tail, which distorts data-strategy decisions for rare-category applications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compositing-artifact learning is discussed for image forensics, but its role in inflating copy-paste detection gains may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with and without copy-paste, evaluate both on natural rare-class test instances and on composited instances with controlled artifact levels, and compare gain profiles.
main_risk: Building genuinely artifact-minimal composites for the control condition is technically demanding and imperfect controls would blur the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Copy-paste gains are attributed to increased effective sample size for rare categories.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Any consistent statistical signature of the augmentation process is a learnable shortcut feature, and pasted-object boundaries are exactly such a signature co-occurring with the boosted labels.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one copy-paste-trained public model separately on natural versus pasted rare-class instances and compare its firing behavior in one session.

one_line_idea: Long-tail detectors have no usable operating point: score miscalibration across the frequency spectrum means any fixed threshold either buries the tail or floods head-class false positives, a deployment failure hidden by AP.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deployed systems require a score threshold, and long-tail detection evaluation reports threshold-free AP averaged over classes without asking whether a single workable operating point exists.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For current long-tail detectors, per-class score distributions are so misaligned across the frequency spectrum that the best global threshold leaves tail classes essentially undetected in operation, so systems that look improved by tail AP are operationally indistinguishable from baselines at any realistic threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping global thresholds on public long-tail detectors and reporting per-stratum operating recall will show a regime where tail recall is near zero until the threshold is so low that head-class false positives per image become operationally unacceptable.
why_important: This translates the long-tail evaluation abstraction into deployment truth, and would justify making operating-point-aware metrics mandatory for long-tail detection claims.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Deployment-threshold analysis specialized to the class-frequency dimension of long-tail detection appears rare in the literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several public models on a long-tail benchmark, sweep global thresholds, plot per-frequency-stratum recall against head-class false positives per image, and compare achievable operating envelopes across methods.
main_risk: Some applications can use per-class thresholds, which weakens the global-threshold framing, so the analysis should report both regimes explicitly.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher tail AP is assumed to translate into better tail detection in deployed operation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: AP integrates over the whole score range including operationally unusable regions, so it can register improvements that exist only below any deployable threshold.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one model, compute tail-stratum recall at the threshold yielding one false positive per ten images, and compare with the AP narrative in a single analysis pass.

one_line_idea: Repeat-factor sampling helps through contexts, not instances: oversampling images containing rare classes mostly benefits by re-exposing their scene contexts, which context-only controls can demonstrate.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Image-level resampling schemes oversample entire images containing rare categories, which simultaneously increases exposure to the rare instances and to their surrounding scenes and co-occurring objects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A significant fraction of the benefit attributed to rare-instance repetition actually comes from re-exposure to rare-class contexts, so a control that oversamples similar contexts without the rare instances, or masks the instances during repeated epochs, retains much of the gain, revealing that the mechanism is context prior sharpening rather than instance learning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training runs comparing standard repeat-factor sampling against instance-masked context oversampling will show the masked variant retaining a nontrivial share of the tail AP gain, contradicting the pure instance-exposure explanation.
why_important: Understanding the causal channel changes what better long-tail training looks like, context synthesis is far cheaper than rare-instance collection, and it also warns that gains may not transfer out of familiar contexts.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ablations of resampling schemes exist, but a causal decomposition of resampling benefits into instance versus context channels via masking interventions may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched trainings with standard oversampling, instance-masked oversampling, and no oversampling, then compare tail AP and its context-stratified breakdown across the three arms.
main_risk: Masking introduces its own artifacts and removes co-occurrence signal in an unnatural way, so several masking styles should be compared to avoid artifact-driven conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Resampling is believed to work by giving the model more gradient signal on rare-class instances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The loss on repeated images is dominated by the many non-rare objects and background patterns in them, so most of the extra gradient actually targets context, not the rare instances.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune a trained baseline briefly with instance-masked rare-context oversampling and check for tail AP movement in a short training run.

one_line_idea: Tail-class names are unstable coordinates: rare-category text embeddings shift wildly across synonyms and phrasing, making vision-language long-tail detection fragile in exactly the classes it claims to fix.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language detectors classify via text embeddings, and rare category names occur infrequently in caption corpora, giving the text encoder little evidence to place them stably in embedding space.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The variance of detection performance under synonym and phrasing substitution is much larger for tail classes than head classes, so vision-language long-tail improvements are brittle, and part of measured tail performance is luck in how the canonical benchmark name happens to embed.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-class AP variance across verified synonym sets will be strongly anticorrelated with class frequency, with tail classes showing swings comparable to their entire claimed improvement over supervised baselines.
why_important: If tail gains depend on name luck, reported long-tail progress from vision-language models is fragile under user vocabulary, and robust naming schemes such as multi-phrase ensembles become necessary components rather than optional tricks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is documented broadly, but its systematic scaling with class frequency in long-tail detection, and the implication for progress claims, may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct verified synonym sets across the frequency spectrum of a long-tail benchmark, evaluate public vision-language detectors under each naming, and regress per-class AP variance on training-name frequency.
main_risk: Rare categories often have few true synonyms, complicating the construction of fair substitution sets for the tail.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A class's zero-shot detection performance is treated as a stable property of the model and the visual category.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Embedding stability comes from training exposure, so the same data scarcity that makes a class rare also makes its coordinate in the classifier space noisy.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one detector on ten tail classes and ten head classes under three phrasings each and compare the per-class spreads in one inference session.

one_line_idea: Average tail AP hides intra-tail regression: long-tail methods improve some rare classes while actively degrading others, and worst-group reporting would change which methods look best.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Long-tail results are summarized as mean AP over frequency strata, and means cannot distinguish uniform improvement from a mixture of gains and losses across the tail classes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Existing long-tail methods redistribute performance within the tail, improving classes that suit their mechanism while hurting others below baseline, so worst-group and per-class-delta reporting would reveal method profiles that mean-based leaderboards conflate, and would reorder methods for applications caring about all rare classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-class delta analysis of public long-tail methods against a shared baseline will show a substantial fraction of tail classes with negative deltas for every method, and rankings under worst-decile tail AP will differ from rankings under mean tail AP.
why_important: Applications with safety-critical rare classes need guarantees on the worst classes, not means, and current reporting invisibly trades some rare classes against others.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Worst-group analysis is standard in robustness literature but appears not to be a norm in long-tail detection reporting.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a baseline and evaluate several long-tail methods per class, publish the per-class delta distributions, and compare mean-based versus worst-group-based method rankings.
main_risk: Per-class estimates in the tail are noisy, interacting with the statistical vacuity problem, so deltas need uncertainty quantification before ranking claims.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A method with higher mean tail AP is assumed better for rare categories across the board.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mechanisms like margin adjustment or sampling reweighting shift decision boundaries globally, and boundary shifts that help contested classes necessarily hurt their neighbors in feature space.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class deltas of one prominent long-tail method against its own reported baseline from cached predictions and count negatively affected tail classes.

one_line_idea: The tail gap decomposes into proposal recall versus classification differently than assumed: for unusual-shaped rare objects the real bottleneck is objectness transfer, not naming, inverting the standard decomposition.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Long-tail detection analyses often assume localization transfers from head classes while classification lags, but tail categories include objects whose scale, aspect ratio, and structure differ strongly from head-class statistics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The localization-transfers assumption holds only for tail classes that are geometrically typical, and for the subset of tail classes with atypical geometry, thin structures, extreme aspect ratios, or unusual scales, proposal recall is the dominant bottleneck, so the tail is heterogeneous and needs bifurcated treatment.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing tail-class errors into proposal-stage misses versus naming failures, stratified by geometric typicality relative to head-class statistics, will show the miss-dominated regime concentrated in geometrically atypical classes.
why_important: A one-size long-tail remedy fails if the tail splits into naming-limited and proposal-limited subpopulations, and detecting geometrically unusual rare objects is common in industrial and scientific applications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Error decomposition by class frequency exists, but crossing it with geometric typicality to reveal a heterogeneous tail bottleneck may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class proposal recall and naming accuracy for a long-tail benchmark, define geometric typicality from head-class shape statistics, and test the interaction between typicality and bottleneck type.
main_risk: Proposal recall depends on the specific proposal mechanism, so several detector families should be analyzed before claiming generality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Class-agnostic localization is assumed to generalize to all unseen or rare categories, focusing long-tail research on the classifier.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectness priors are learned from the geometry distribution of annotated training objects, and geometry far outside that distribution is exactly where learned proposal mechanisms have never been supervised.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one detector, list tail classes with lowest proposal recall and check by inspection whether they cluster in atypical geometry, an afternoon of analysis on cached proposals.

one_line_idea: Boxes already contain masks: frozen features of box-only detectors support high-quality mask prediction with tiny mask supervision, suggesting mask annotation budgets are largely wasted.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Instance segmentation is treated as requiring large mask-annotated datasets, while box annotation is far cheaper, and detectors trained with boxes alone learn rich object-boundary-sensitive features as a byproduct.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The information needed for accurate masks is already present in box-trained detector features, so a small mask head trained on a tiny fraction of mask labels atop frozen box-detector features approaches the mask quality of fully mask-supervised models, implying the marginal value of large-scale mask annotation is low.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Mask heads trained on progressively smaller mask-label fractions over frozen box-trained features will show a mask-quality curve that saturates early, reaching within a small margin of full supervision at a small percentage of labels.
why_important: Annotation budgets are a first-order cost in applied vision, and if boxes plus few masks suffice, dataset construction strategy across the field should change.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weakly supervised instance segmentation exists, but a clean label-efficiency saturation analysis specifically probing what box-only training already encodes may not be established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a box-only detector, freeze it, train mask heads with varying mask-label budgets, and plot mask quality against budget compared to end-to-end mask-supervised baselines.
main_risk: Findings may depend on the detector family and the mask head capacity, requiring a small grid over both to support a general claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] High-quality instance segmentation is assumed to need large-scale mask supervision or a dedicated segmentation foundation model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Precise box regression under scale and occlusion variation already forces features to encode object extent and boundary layout, and the mask head only needs to read this out.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Freeze one public box-trained detector, fit a small mask head on a small mask subset, and evaluate mask quality the same week.

one_line_idea: Segmentation-first detection wins on irregular objects: deriving boxes from class-agnostic masks beats box-first pipelines for thin, curved, and perforated objects, an advantage hidden by benchmark shape statistics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The dominant pipeline predicts boxes first and optionally refines masks, and axis-aligned boxes are a poor summary for thin or non-convex objects where most box area is background.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For an identifiable shape subpopulation, boxes-from-masks pipelines outperform box-first ones on both localization and downstream usefulness, and mainstream benchmarks contain too few such objects for this advantage to register in overall AP, so pipeline-design conclusions drawn from benchmark averages are shape-biased.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Shape-stratified evaluation, using mask-derived measures like convexity and elongation, will show a consistent regime where mask-first pipelines dominate box-first ones, and the size of this stratum varies drastically across application domains.
why_important: Cabling, tools, plants, cracks, and biological structures are everyday irregular objects; if pipeline superiority is shape-dependent, engineering guidance should be conditional on shape statistics rather than universal.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mask-versus-box pipeline comparisons exist per-benchmark, but a shape-stratified analysis establishing a crossover regime may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate matched mask-first and box-first pipelines on datasets with mask ground truth, stratify all metrics by shape statistics, and locate the crossover in shape space.
main_risk: Confounding between shape and category semantics is strong, so analysis should compare within categories that span shape diversity where possible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Box-first detection is treated as the default backbone of localization pipelines, with masks as an optional refinement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For a thin diagonal object, the box IoU signal barely constrains the object at all, so training and evaluating through boxes discards most localization information exactly where objects are hardest.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Stratify existing benchmark results of one mask-first and one box-first public model by ground-truth mask convexity and compare the orderings per stratum in an analysis session.

one_line_idea: Interior-dominated mask metrics hide boundary failure: instance segmentation progress measured by mask IoU has plateaued at boundaries, and boundary-weighted evaluation reorders methods and better predicts downstream utility.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Mask IoU is dominated by interior pixels for all but tiny objects, so two masks with very different boundary quality can score nearly identically, and applications like grasping, editing, and measurement depend disproportionately on boundaries.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Ranking instance segmentation methods by boundary-focused metrics diverges materially from mask-IoU rankings, boundary quality has improved much more slowly than interior quality over recent method generations, and boundary metrics predict downstream task success better than mask IoU does.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-evaluating a pool of public instance segmentation models under boundary-weighted metrics will show ranking divergence from mask IoU, and a downstream proxy task using masks will correlate more with boundary scores than with mask IoU.
why_important: If the standard metric is boundary-blind, the field may be saturating an easy component while the operationally critical component stagnates unmeasured.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Boundary metrics exist, but a systematic cross-generation audit tying boundary stagnation to metric blindness and downstream utility may not have been assembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score multiple public models spanning several method generations under both metric families, quantify ranking divergence and per-generation progress rates, and validate against one concrete downstream task.
main_risk: Boundary metrics are sensitive to annotation boundary noise, so the analysis must estimate the annotation noise floor to avoid over-interpreting differences.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mask AP improvements are read as across-the-board segmentation quality improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Metric mass concentrates where pixels are, interiors, so optimizing models against interior-dominated losses and metrics yields exactly the observed pattern of confident blobs with sloppy edges.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score cached masks of three public models with a boundary-weighted metric and compare orderings against mask IoU in one afternoon.

one_line_idea: Detector-to-segmenter pipelines fail multiplicatively, not independently: promptable segmenters amplify detector box errors on exactly the hard instances, so pipeline quality is worse than the product of component qualities.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A common modern pipeline feeds detector boxes as prompts to a promptable segmentation model, and both components are evaluated in isolation on different benchmarks with independent error statistics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detector box errors and prompt-conditioned segmentation errors are positively correlated on the same instances, occlusion, clutter, and ambiguous extent hurt both stages, so end-to-end mask quality is substantially below what independence-based composition of component metrics predicts, and component-wise model selection misranks full pipelines.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring end-to-end pipeline mask quality against a prediction composed from component-wise error rates under independence will show a systematic shortfall, concentrated on instances flagged hard for the detector.
why_important: Teams select detectors and segmenters from separate leaderboards assuming composability; correlated failure means the best pipeline may use components that are individually suboptimal but complementary.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pipeline error compounding is a classic systems concern, but a quantitative correlated-failure analysis for the now-standard detect-then-prompt-segment stack may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several detector-segmenter combinations end to end on a mask-annotated benchmark, model expected pipeline quality from component metrics under independence, and measure the correlation structure of stage-wise errors per instance.
main_risk: Defining stage-wise error attribution requires care when the segmenter partially recovers from bad prompts, needing a sensible attribution protocol.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Best-in-class detector plus best-in-class segmenter is assumed to give the best pipeline.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The instance properties that make a box wrong, ambiguous extent and occlusion, are the same properties that make prompt-conditioned mask inference ambiguous, guaranteeing error correlation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one pipeline on one benchmark, scatter per-instance detector box IoU against final mask IoU and inspect the joint distribution for correlated failure in one session.

one_line_idea: Amodal-modal convention mismatch breaks detection-segmentation stacks under occlusion: components trained with different visibility conventions disagree precisely on occluded objects, and pipelines silently mix the two.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Some annotation conventions cover only visible pixels while others include occluded extent, and detectors and segmenters trained under different conventions are now freely combined in pipelines.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detector boxes and segmenter masks in mixed-convention pipelines diverge systematically as occlusion increases, producing box-mask inconsistencies that harm downstream geometry estimates, and occlusion-stratified consistency measurement will expose which popular component combinations are convention-incompatible.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Box-mask consistency of popular pipeline combinations will degrade monotonically with occlusion fraction, with degradation rates differing by combination in ways predicted by their training conventions rather than by their component qualities.
why_important: Robotics and driving stacks consume boxes and masks jointly for spatial reasoning, and convention-driven inconsistency under occlusion corrupts exactly the safety-relevant crowded cases.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Amodal segmentation is its own research thread, but a convention-compatibility audit of mixed detection-segmentation pipelines may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble occlusion-annotated evaluation data, run pipeline combinations spanning training conventions, and quantify box-mask consistency and downstream extent-estimation error versus occlusion level.
main_risk: Occlusion levels need ground-truth annotation or reliable estimation, and mixed conventions inside single training datasets could blur the attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Boxes and masks from strong models are assumed mutually consistent views of the same object.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Under occlusion the visible-pixel answer and the full-extent answer are genuinely different geometric objects, so components trained to different conventions must disagree, no matter how good each is.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run one popular pipeline on obviously occluded instances and plot box-mask containment statistics against a rough occlusion score within a day.

one_line_idea: Training detection through mask-derived objectives improves boxes themselves: replacing box regression targets with boxes derived from predicted masks yields better localization even measured by box AP on non-convex objects.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Box regression treats the rectangle as the primitive, forcing the model to learn a shape summary chosen for annotation convenience, and rectangle corners are weakly constrained by visual evidence for irregular objects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Predicting spatial support first and deriving boxes from it provides a better-posed learning signal, so mask-mediated box training improves box quality on irregular and occluded objects relative to direct box regression at matched supervision cost, because the intermediate representation aligns with actual evidence.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matched trainings with direct box regression versus mask-mediated box derivation, using only box-consistent supervision, will show the mask-mediated variant ahead on high-IoU box metrics for non-convex and occluded strata.
why_important: If the rectangle is a bad learning primitive, a large fraction of detector training practice is anchored on a representational mistake that costs localization quality for hard shapes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Boxes-from-masks exists as an inference trick, but a controlled claim that mask mediation improves box learning itself under box-only supervision budgets may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement both training modes on one architecture with matched budgets, evaluate box quality stratified by shape convexity and occlusion, and check the predicted advantage pattern.
main_risk: Mask mediation without mask labels needs weak mask learning from boxes, whose failure could contaminate the comparison, so a mask-supervised upper-bound arm is needed for reference.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Direct box regression is treated as the natural and sufficient way to learn localization when boxes are the target output.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The corners of a box on a diagonal thin object sit in empty background, so direct regression asks the network to predict positions with no local evidence, whereas support prediction grounds every output in observable pixels.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare high-IoU box AP of an existing mask-capable model's mask-derived boxes against its own regressed boxes on non-convex categories using cached outputs.

one_line_idea: Instance segmentation systematically forbids nested instances: overlap-resolution heuristics assume quasi-disjoint objects, making object-inside-object cases a structural blind spot across current methods.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Instance segmentation pipelines resolve overlapping predictions through suppression and pixel-assignment rules that softly enforce near-disjoint instance supports, while real scenes contain nested instances such as contents inside containers, pictures within pictures, and components within assemblies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Current methods fail on nested-instance configurations at rates far above their overall error rates, the failure is caused by overlap-resolution machinery rather than by features, and benchmarks under-sample nesting so severely that this structural limitation has escaped measurement.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a purpose-built nested-instance test suite, methods will show a characteristic failure signature, suppression of the inner instance or merging into the outer one, and disabling or relaxing overlap resolution will recover many inner instances at some precision cost.
why_important: Nesting is routine in industrial inspection, retail, and document-like scenes, and a structural inability to represent it caps the applicability of instance segmentation regardless of feature quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Overlap handling is discussed as engineering detail, but naming and measuring the nested-instance blind spot as a category of failure may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or photograph a nested-instance test set with unambiguous annotations, evaluate a spectrum of public methods, and ablate overlap-resolution components to localize the cause.
main_risk: Annotation conventions for nesting are genuinely ambiguous in some cases, requiring a tight instance-definition protocol before measurement.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Instance segmentation failures are attributed to feature or supervision limits, with overlap resolution assumed benign.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A pixel-assignment rule that gives each pixel to one instance cannot express one object being part of the visual support of another, so the representation, not the learning, forbids the correct answer.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Photograph a few dozen container-content scenes, run two public models, and count inner-instance recoveries with and without suppression in a day.

one_line_idea: Detection-segmentation multitask benefit is one-directional: detection supervision helps segmentation, but segmentation supervision adds little to detection at foundation scale, contradicting the mutual-benefit narrative.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multitask training of detection and segmentation is commonly justified by mutual benefit claims established in the era of small models and datasets, and modern foundation-scale training changes the marginal value of auxiliary supervision.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At current pretraining scale, the marginal benefit matrix between detection and segmentation supervision is strongly asymmetric, box supervision still improves mask tasks, while mask supervision contributes negligibly or negatively to box tasks, so joint-training design decisions based on old mutual-benefit results are miscalibrated.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A controlled supervision-ablation grid on a modern backbone, adding each task's labels incrementally to the other's training, will show clearly asymmetric transfer, with mask-to-box gains within noise while box-to-mask gains remain solid.
why_important: Mask annotation is expensive; if it does not help detection, budget-constrained projects should not buy masks for detection quality, and multitask architectures should not be motivated by symmetric synergy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multitask synergy was documented on older stacks, and a re-measurement of the transfer matrix at foundation scale with modern recipes may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the two-way supervision ablation at fixed compute on one modern architecture and dataset, with repeated seeds, and report the transfer matrix with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Findings could be architecture-specific, motivating replication across one query-based and one dense detector at minimum.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detection and segmentation are assumed mutually reinforcing tasks whose joint training benefits both.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Box localization information is a strict subset of mask information, so masks can substitute for boxes, but at scale the backbone may already saturate the spatial features that masks would add, leaving nothing for masks to teach detection.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one pretrained backbone for detection with and without an auxiliary mask loss at matched compute and compare box AP over a few seeds.

one_line_idea: The thing-stuff boundary is a load-bearing arbitrary choice: reclassifying ambiguous categories between thing and stuff swings panoptic comparisons, so panoptic rankings partly measure ontology luck.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Panoptic evaluation splits categories into countable things and amorphous stuff, applying different matching and scoring rules to each, and several real-world categories, crowds, piles, vegetation, wires, admit either treatment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method rankings under panoptic metrics are sensitive to the thing-stuff assignment of ambiguous categories, because architectures differ in relative instance versus semantic strength, so a plausible re-partition of the ontology changes leaderboard order, revealing that part of measured quality is fit to one ontology choice.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-scoring public panoptic models under several defensible thing-stuff re-partitions will change method gaps materially and flip at least some adjacent rankings, with instance-strong methods favored by thing-heavy ontologies and vice versa.
why_important: Cross-paper panoptic comparisons and architectural conclusions inherit the ontology silently; showing rank sensitivity would force ontology-robust reporting or explicit per-partition claims.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ontology sensitivity of panoptic evaluation seems undocumented as a measured ranking-stability problem.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define several ambiguous-category re-partitions with independent human justification, re-score cached outputs of public panoptic models under each, and quantify rank stability.
main_risk: Re-scoring requires models to produce outputs compatible with both treatments for the moved categories, which may need light output adaptation and careful fairness arguments.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The benchmark ontology is treated as ground truth, and panoptic scores are read as ontology-independent quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Countability is a property of human linguistic convention as much as of visual structure, so any fixed partition encodes contestable choices that interact with architecture biases.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Move the two or three most obviously ambiguous categories across the boundary, re-score two public models, and check the gap movement in one analysis session.

one_line_idea: Segmenter stability is a better detection confidence than the detector's own score: rescoring detections by mask agreement under prompt jitter improves ranking quality without retraining anything.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detector confidence scores are learned artifacts of training losses and calibrate poorly, while promptable segmenters provide a cheap independent probe, the stability of the mask they produce under perturbed prompts around a detection.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For a true detection, jittered box prompts converge to consistent masks, while for false positives mask outputs vary erratically, so a stability score computed from a few jittered prompts reranks detections better than the native confidence, improving AP and especially precision at deployment thresholds, with no training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Replacing or blending detector confidence with prompt-jitter mask-consistency scores will improve AP and high-precision operating points across several detector-segmenter pairs, with the largest gains on cluttered scenes.
why_important: A training-free, architecture-agnostic confidence repair would immediately benefit every deployed detect-and-segment stack and would reframe segmenters as verification tools, not just mask producers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Using promptable segmentation stability as a detection verification signal may be unexplored as a systematic rescoring method.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement jitter-based stability scoring over public detector-segmenter pairs, evaluate rescored detections on standard benchmarks, and ablate the number of jittered prompts against gain.
main_risk: Inference cost multiplies with prompt count, and stability may fail exactly on ambiguous-boundary true objects, requiring analysis of where the signal helps versus harms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detection confidence is taken as the best available ranking signal, with segmentation viewed as a downstream consumer rather than an upstream verifier.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask stability measures agreement of independent conditional inferences about object support, a genuinely different evidence channel than the classification-head score, so it can correct confidence errors the detector cannot see.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one detector-segmenter pair on one benchmark subset, compute stability scores with five jitters and compare precision-recall against native confidence in a day.

one_line_idea: Dense pretraining transfers to detection through objectness, not classification: pixel-level pretraining gains concentrate in proposal recall, implying cheap class-agnostic dense objectives could replace expensive semantic ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense self-supervised and segmentation-oriented pretraining improves downstream detection, and the standard explanation credits better semantic features, without decomposing where in the detection pipeline the gain lands.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant channel of dense-pretraining benefit for detection is improved class-agnostic objectness and boundary sensitivity rather than improved region classification, so decomposed evaluation will locate the gains in proposal recall and localization precision, and a purely class-agnostic dense objective will match semantic dense pretraining for detection transfer.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing matched backbones with dense-semantic versus dense-class-agnostic versus image-level pretraining will show the two dense variants clustering together on proposal recall and box quality, both ahead of image-level, with little difference in classification accuracy given oracle boxes.
why_important: If semantics are not the operative ingredient, dense pretraining can be simplified and scaled cheaply, and the community's interpretation of why segmentation-flavored pretraining helps detection needs revision.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Transfer studies compare endpoints, but a stage-decomposed attribution of dense-pretraining benefits within the detection pipeline may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain or gather matched backbones under the three objective families, fine-tune identically, and report stage-decomposed detection metrics, proposal recall, localization precision, and oracle-box classification.
main_risk: Public checkpoints differ in data and compute, so credible attribution likely requires controlled pretraining at moderate scale.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense pretraining is thought to help detection by producing semantically richer local features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection classification operates on pooled region features where image-level pretraining already excels, while proposal generation needs precisely the local boundary structure that only dense objectives are forced to represent.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare proposal recall and oracle-box classification separately for two public backbones, one dense-pretrained and one image-level, under one fine-tuning recipe.

one_line_idea: Foundation-distilled pseudo-masks carry a convexity bias that survives training: models trained on segmenter-generated masks inherit systematically inflated, smoothed object supports, capping thin-structure segmentation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] It is now common to generate training masks at scale by prompting segmentation foundation models, and generated masks exhibit characteristic error styles rather than unbiased noise.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation-generated pseudo-masks are biased toward convex, smoothed supports that bridge thin gaps and clip protrusions, student models trained on them inherit and amplify this bias, and the resulting ceiling on thin-structure quality persists even when large fractions of clean labels are mixed in.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Statistical comparison of pseudo-masks against expert annotation will show directional convexity and boundary-smoothing biases, and students trained on pseudo-masks will replicate the bias on held-out data, with thin-structure recall degrading relative to students trained on expert masks at matched volume.
why_important: Pseudo-labeling is becoming the default scaling path for segmentation data, and directional label bias, unlike random noise, does not wash out with volume, threatening a field-wide inherited artifact.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pseudo-label noise is widely acknowledged, but characterizing it as a directional shape bias with demonstrated inheritance in students may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantify shape-statistic deltas between foundation-generated and expert masks on a common image set, train students on each, and measure bias inheritance and thin-structure performance on expert-annotated tests.
main_risk: Bias profiles differ across prompting modes and segmenter versions, requiring a matrix of generation settings for generality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Foundation-generated masks are treated as approximately unbiased noisy labels whose errors average out at scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generative and interactive segmenters are trained toward typical object supports, so their errors point systematically toward shape priors, and systematic errors are exactly what students learn best.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Generate pseudo-masks for one thin-structure-rich image set, compute convexity and boundary-length statistics against expert masks, and check the directional bias in one session.

one_line_idea: Attribute binding fails at the instance level in open-vocabulary detection: with two objects of swapped attributes in one scene, detectors match queries to the wrong instances at near-chance rates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contrastive vision-language models exhibit bag-of-words behavior at image level, and open-vocabulary detectors inherit their text encoders and alignment objectives while claiming instance-level language grounding.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Region-text alignment does not repair compositional binding, so in scenes containing two instances whose attributes are exchanged, a red cup beside a blue plate versus a blue cup beside a red plate, queries specifying attribute-noun combinations select the correct instance barely above chance, even when each attribute and noun is individually well detected.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a swapped-attribute two-instance test suite, instance-selection accuracy for compositional queries will be far below single-object attribute recognition accuracy, exposing binding, not perception, as the failing capability.
why_important: Instance-level language grounding is the core advertised capability distinguishing open-vocabulary detection from classification, and binding failure means multi-object scenes cannot be reliably queried, which is the typical deployment case.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Binding failures are established at image level, and a clean instance-level binding benchmark for detection with chance-level baselines may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct or photograph swapped-attribute scene pairs, verify single-object attribute recognition as a control, and measure compositional instance selection across public open-vocabulary detectors.
main_risk: Scene construction must avoid incidental cues, position or size correlations, that let models shortcut the binding test.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Region-level training is assumed to fix image-level compositionality failures because regions isolate single objects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attribute-object binding must happen inside the query embedding before matching, and the text encoder that failed image-level binding produces the same order-insensitive embedding for region matching.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Assemble a few dozen swapped-attribute composites, run one public detector, and measure instance-selection accuracy against chance in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Web-pretrained detectors hallucinate companion objects: scores for typically co-occurring categories are elevated even when absent, and this co-occurrence hallucination exceeds that of in-domain supervised detectors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web image-caption data encodes strong object co-occurrence statistics, and caption supervision rewards predicting plausible scene descriptions, creating pressure toward co-occurrence-based inference.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation detectors assign systematically elevated detection scores to absent-but-typical companion objects, a keyboard near a monitor, a rider on a horse, relative to matched supervised detectors, and the effect strength is predictable from co-occurrence statistics of the pretraining distribution.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On curated scenes containing one member of a high-co-occurrence pair with the partner verifiably absent, foundation detectors will produce partner false positives at rates exceeding supervised baselines, ordered by pair co-occurrence strength.
why_important: Hallucinated companions are confident structured false positives that downstream logic happily consumes, and knowing that web pretraining increases this failure changes the safety calculus of adopting foundation detectors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contextual hallucination is known qualitatively, but a controlled comparison attributing elevated companion hallucination specifically to web-scale caption pretraining may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate partner-absent scenes for a range of co-occurrence strengths, evaluate matched foundation and supervised detectors, and regress partner false-positive rates on co-occurrence statistics per model family.
main_risk: Verifying absence rigorously and matching detector pairs on accuracy are both essential and nontrivial for a fair attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More and broader pretraining data is expected to reduce hallucination by improving perception.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Caption likelihood is maximized by predicting typical scenes, so the pretraining objective actively installs the co-occurrence prior that later masquerades as detection evidence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Test a handful of iconic pairs with partner-absent images on one foundation and one supervised detector and compare partner score distributions in a day.

one_line_idea: Typographic attacks transfer from classification to open-vocabulary detection: text written in the scene shifts region scores, so rendered words act as adversarial detection evidence.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contrastive image-text models are known to read rendered text in images and conflate it with visual content at image level, and open-vocabulary detectors reuse these vision encoders for region-level scoring.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Rendered text influences open-vocabulary detection at region level, boosting scores of the written category in regions near or containing the text, so signs, labels, and packaging text systematically distort detection, and adversaries can plant detections with a marker pen.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Adding category words to scenes, physically or synthetically, will raise false-positive rates of those categories in text-bearing regions across public open-vocabulary detectors, with the effect surviving realistic text sizes and placements.
why_important: Text is everywhere in built environments, so this is not only an adversarial threat but an everyday distribution property, menus, storefronts, and packaging would bias detection continuously.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Typographic attacks are established for classification, and their region-level transfer, everyday-distortion framing, and physical realizability for detection may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired scenes with and without planted category text at varying sizes and positions, evaluate several detectors, and map the spatial footprint of score inflation around text.
main_risk: Effects may vary strongly across detector families depending on how their region features pool text evidence, requiring a family-stratified analysis.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detection scores are read as reflecting object appearance evidence within the region.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The vision encoder was rewarded during pretraining for matching images to captions partly via rendered text, and region pooling inherits whatever text-sensitive features it built.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Write category names on paper, photograph them inside ordinary scenes, and run one detector to compare scores against text-free controls in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Foundation detector errors are correlated across model families: shared web data induces shared blind spots, so ensembling different foundation detectors yields far less error diversity than their architectural diversity suggests.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Ensembling and cross-model verification assume some independence of errors, and the major foundation detectors are trained on heavily overlapping web-derived corpora despite differing architectures and recipes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Instance-level error overlap between distinct foundation detector families substantially exceeds what accuracy-matched independence would predict, exceeds the overlap between supervised detectors trained on disjoint data, and concentrates on data-driven failure modes, so consensus among foundation models is much weaker evidence of correctness than assumed.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Pairwise error-overlap analysis on a common benchmark will show foundation-model pairs clustering well above the independence baseline, and ensemble gains across foundation families will fall clearly short of gains predicted from their individual accuracies.
why_important: Safety cases and auto-labeling pipelines increasingly rely on multi-model agreement; correlated blind spots silently break these designs precisely on the shared-data failure modes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Error correlation is studied within ensembles generally, but a data-lineage-focused audit of cross-family error correlation for detection foundation models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several foundation and supervised detectors on common benchmarks, compute instance-level error overlap against accuracy-matched independence nulls, and measure realized versus predicted ensemble gains.
main_risk: Disentangling data-driven from task-driven error correlation requires supervised controls on disjoint data, which constrains dataset choices.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Different model families are assumed to fail differently, making cross-model agreement strong evidence of correctness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Failure modes live largely in the data distribution, and when everyone trains on the same web, they inherit the same holes regardless of architecture.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute the instance-level joint error table for two foundation detectors on one benchmark and compare against the independence prediction in one analysis session.

one_line_idea: Foundation detectors have a canonical-scale prior: objects photographed at atypical absolute scales, extreme close-ups or extreme distance, are missed in ways predicted by web photo composition statistics, and rescaling recovers them.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web photographs frame objects at conventional scales driven by human photographic habits, and foundation detectors consume this distribution during pretraining, while deployment imagery, inspection close-ups, wide-area monitoring, violates those conventions routinely.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation detectors encode a per-category canonical apparent-size prior, so detection performance as a function of object apparent size peaks near web-typical framing and degrades asymmetrically at atypical scales, and simple test-time rescaling toward the canonical size recovers a large share of the misses, proving the failure is a prior, not a feature limitation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-category performance-versus-apparent-size curves for foundation detectors will peak near category-typical web framing, and rescaled inference will recover substantially more detections for foundation detectors than for supervised detectors trained on scale-augmented data.
why_important: Applications with unusual optics inherit a hidden penalty from web pretraining conventions, and the recovery-by-rescaling result would provide both a diagnosis and a cheap deployable mitigation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale robustness is an old topic, but tying category-specific scale response curves to web framing statistics with a rescaling-based causal test may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-category size-response curves on size-diverse test data, estimate category-typical framing statistics from a public caption corpus sample, correlate the two, and test rescaled inference recovery.
main_risk: Apparent size confounds with blur, depth of field, and context availability, so optical controls or synthetic rescaling protocols are needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Web-scale pretraining diversity is assumed to confer broad scale invariance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pretraining diversity covers what photographers shoot, and photographers shoot conventionally, so the diversity is narrower in scale-space than its volume suggests.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Photograph familiar objects at several unusual scales, run one foundation detector at native and canonically rescaled resolutions, and compare recovery in a day.

one_line_idea: Foundation detectors are right for the wrong pixels: attribution analysis shows their class decisions rely on context outside the box far more than supervised detectors, predicting brittleness that in-box-only evaluation misses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection evaluation scores box-label pairs without asking which pixels drove the decision, and caption-supervised pretraining rewards whole-image inference, unlike box-supervised training which localizes credit.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For matched correct detections, the causal contribution of outside-box pixels to the classification decision is systematically higher in foundation detectors than in supervised ones, and this reliance predicts which detections break under context perturbation, making evidence-localization a measurable robustness indicator that current metrics ignore.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Context-masking and context-shuffling interventions will degrade foundation-detector decisions on previously correct detections at higher rates than supervised-detector decisions, and per-detection outside-box reliance scores will predict which detections flip.
why_important: Two detectors with identical AP can differ hugely in where their evidence comes from, and evidence localization determines robustness to scene changes, so it should become a reported dimension of detector quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context reliance has been studied for CNN-era detectors, and a foundation-versus-supervised evidence-localization comparison with predictive validity for perturbation robustness may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute outside-box reliance via masking interventions for matched detections across model families, then measure flip rates under independent context perturbations and test the predictive relationship.
main_risk: Masking artifacts themselves perturb models, so multiple intervention styles, blur, shuffle, inpaint, must agree before attributing reliance.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A correct high-confidence detection is treated as evidence the model perceived the object itself.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Caption supervision never told the model where the object was, so gradient pressure built whole-scene shortcuts that region heads inherit even after detection fine-tuning.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Mask outside-box context for a sample of correct detections from one foundation and one supervised model and compare decision-flip rates in one session.

one_line_idea: Frozen foundation features hit a localization precision ceiling: high-IoU detection quality saturates regardless of head capacity, because image-level pretraining discards sub-patch spatial precision that fine-tuning must rebuild.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Frozen-backbone detection is attractive for efficiency and multi-task reuse, and patch-based foundation encoders summarize local content at patch granularity optimized for semantic, not geometric, objectives.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detection heads on frozen foundation features show a characteristic signature, competitive low-IoU AP but a persistent deficit at high IoU thresholds that no head capacity increase closes, while modest backbone fine-tuning closes it quickly, demonstrating that precise extent information is absent from frozen features rather than merely unread.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping head capacity over frozen backbones will asymptote high-IoU AP well below the same architecture with backbone tuning, and the frozen-versus-tuned gap will concentrate sharply in the highest IoU bands and smallest objects.
why_important: The frozen-backbone paradigm underpins efficient deployment and foundation-model-as-a-service designs, and a structural localization ceiling defines exactly which applications that paradigm cannot serve.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frozen-versus-tuned comparisons exist as single numbers, but the IoU-resolved saturation analysis with head-capacity sweeps isolating information absence may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train head-capacity sweeps over frozen and lightly tuned backbones under one recipe, report IoU-threshold-resolved AP curves, and test whether the frozen asymptote stays below tuned performance at high IoU.
main_risk: Multi-scale feature extraction tricks from intermediate layers might recover precision without tuning, so the study must include strong frozen-feature-engineering baselines to avoid a strawman.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Frozen foundation features are assumed sufficient for detection given a good enough head, with fine-tuning framed as an optional accuracy bonus.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Information destroyed by patch-level pooling during pretraining cannot be recreated by any head, no matter its capacity, and semantic objectives give no reason to preserve sub-patch geometry.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare IoU-resolved AP curves of one frozen-backbone and one tuned-backbone detector already available publicly, checking whether the gap concentrates at high IoU.

one_line_idea: Foundation detectors have a web-aesthetic prior: semantically harmless but statistically atypical imaging conditions, unusual white balance, nonstandard aspect ratios, flash artifacts, degrade them more than matched supervised detectors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness testing for detection uses canonical corruption suites modeled on photographic degradations, while web pretraining data carries a strong selection bias toward aesthetically conventional, post-processed imagery.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation detectors are tuned to web-typical image statistics beyond semantics, so distribution shifts that violate web aesthetics without harming semantic content cause disproportionate degradation relative to supervised detectors trained with aggressive photometric augmentation, and standard corruption benchmarks miss this axis entirely.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a shift suite of semantically transparent but web-atypical conditions, raw sensor renderings, unusual color temperature, security-camera-style processing, foundation detectors will lose more relative performance than supervised baselines, while both degrade similarly on the canonical corruption suite.
why_important: Deployment imagery, industrial, medical, surveillance, is systematically web-atypical, so this hidden prior taxes exactly the sectors adopting foundation detectors fastest, and robustness reporting based on canonical corruptions provides false assurance.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Corruption robustness of detectors is well studied, but isolating the web-aesthetic selection bias as a distinct shift axis with a purpose-built suite may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct the web-atypical shift suite via raw-image reprocessing pipelines, evaluate matched foundation and supervised detectors on both suites, and compare relative degradation profiles.
main_risk: Constructing shifts that are truly semantically transparent requires human verification that recognizability is preserved.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Web-scale pretraining is expected to dominate supervised training on any distribution shift due to sheer data diversity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web data diversity is bounded by the upload-and-curation funnel, which filters toward processed, well-composed imagery, making the effective training distribution narrower in imaging-statistics space than in content space.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Reprocess one test set through a raw-style rendering pipeline and compare relative AP drops of one foundation and one supervised detector in a day.

one_line_idea: Multimodal LLMs are better detection verifiers than detectors: their box generation fails on coordinate production, not perception, so the generation-verification gap argues for verifier-role deployment.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal language models are increasingly asked to output bounding boxes as text, and producing numeric coordinates through a language head is a very different computation from judging a shown box.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For the same model and images, the accuracy of accepting or rejecting proposed boxes substantially exceeds the accuracy of generating boxes, the generation deficit traces to coordinate-production errors rather than perceptual failure, and a proposal-plus-LLM-verification pipeline therefore beats LLM-direct detection at matched compute.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring generation quality versus verification quality on matched instances will show a wide gap favoring verification, and error analysis of generated boxes will attribute most loss to systematic coordinate distortions rather than to wrong-object selection.
why_important: Teams are wiring multimodal LLMs into localization roles they perform poorly, while the verification capability that could improve existing detectors goes unused, so establishing the gap redirects system design.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Generation-verification asymmetries are discussed for text reasoning, and a quantitative perceptual-versus-production decomposition for multimodal localization may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several multimodal LLMs, measure box generation quality, box verification quality on controlled positive and negative proposals, and reconstruct the generation loss decomposition via perturbation analysis of coordinates versus object identity.
main_risk: Verification probes can leak answer statistics through proposal construction, so negative proposals need careful stratified design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multimodal LLM localization failures are read as perceptual grounding failures.
