why_it_might_be_wrong: Emitting precise numerals autoregressively is a known weak channel for language models, and the perception could be intact behind a broken output interface.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one multimodal LLM, compare its box-drawing accuracy against its accept-reject accuracy on the same fifty objects in one session.

one_line_idea: Multimodal LLM boxes betray tokenizer priors: generated coordinates cluster on round numbers and canonical aspect ratios, a measurable output-distribution distortion that standard AP evaluation never reveals.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Language-model detection outputs are produced as token sequences, and token frequency statistics from pretraining favor round and common numerals, while true box coordinates are near-uniformly distributed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Generated box distributions from multimodal LLMs exhibit strong spectral peaks at round coordinates, quantization-grid artifacts, and aspect-ratio modes absent from ground-truth distributions, these distortions bias which objects are localizable accurately, and distributional distortion severity predicts per-model localization quality on non-canonical geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing generated-coordinate distributions against ground truth will show significant round-number and grid clustering for language-head models but not for regression-head detectors, and per-instance localization error will correlate with distance of the true box from the model's preferred coordinate lattice.
why_important: This identifies a structural output-representation tax on language-based localization, informing both interface design, such as coordinate binning or special tokens, and fair evaluation of multimodal claims about detection ability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Numeral biases are known in text generation, and their geometric consequences for localization output distributions appear unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect large generated-box samples from several multimodal LLMs, run distributional tests against ground truth and regression-detector outputs, and correlate lattice distance with per-instance error.
main_risk: Prompt format strongly affects numeric output style, so the analysis must sweep prompting conventions to separate model priors from prompt artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Coordinate emission is treated as a neutral serialization detail of multimodal detection interfaces.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every token emitted is shaped by pretraining frequency statistics, and nothing in fine-tuning volumes typically suffices to flatten numeral priors into uniform coordinate competence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Histogram the final digits and aspect ratios of a few thousand generated boxes from one model against ground truth in a single analysis session.

one_line_idea: Caption-worthiness bias shapes foundation detection: recall as a function of object size, centrality, and photographic salience is steeper for web-pretrained detectors, penalizing peripheral and incidental objects.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Captions describe what photographers and writers deem noteworthy, so region-text supervision concentrates on salient, central, large objects, while detection benchmarks and applications require finding incidental background objects too.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation detectors inherit a caption-worthiness prior, their recall gradient along salience dimensions, centrality, relative size, photographic focus, is systematically steeper than that of box-supervised detectors whose annotation protocols enforced exhaustiveness, and this bias persists after detection fine-tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Salience-stratified recall comparisons at matched overall AP will show foundation detectors losing disproportionately on peripheral, defocused, and incidental instances, with the deficit correlating with estimated caption-mention probability of similar objects.
why_important: Surveillance, safety, and inventory applications care precisely about unremarkable objects nobody would caption, so a caption-worthiness prior is a targeted capability gap hidden inside healthy-looking aggregate metrics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Salience effects on captioning are documented, and their propagation into detection recall profiles as a measured inheritance may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define salience strata from geometry and focus measures, compare recall profiles of matched foundation and supervised detectors, and test correlation with caption-mention statistics estimated from a public corpus.
main_risk: Benchmark annotation itself may under-label incidental objects, so exhaustively re-annotated evaluation subsets are needed for trustworthy stratified recall.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detection fine-tuning is assumed to wash out pretraining biases about which objects matter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning reweights but does not erase representation priorities, and features never built for incidental objects during pretraining leave nothing for fine-tuning to reweight.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Stratify existing benchmark recall by object centrality and relative size for one foundation and one supervised detector using cached predictions.

one_line_idea: Vocabulary forgetting outpaces domain gains: fine-tuning open-vocabulary detectors on narrow domains erases their broad-vocabulary competence at a rate that makes naive domain adaptation a net capability loss.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners routinely fine-tune open-vocabulary detectors on domain data with a small class set, and catastrophic forgetting under narrow fine-tuning is a general neural network phenomenon.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Open-vocabulary breadth degrades faster than domain performance improves along the fine-tuning trajectory, the forgetting is concentrated in the region-text alignment rather than the visual features, and the standard practice of picking checkpoints by domain validation silently selects near-maximal vocabulary damage.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Tracking broad-vocabulary AP and domain AP along fine-tuning will show broad-vocabulary decline crossing domain gains early, and probing experiments will localize the damage to alignment layers, with visual-feature probes remaining largely intact.
why_important: The value proposition of open-vocabulary detectors is breadth plus adaptability; quantifying their trade-off curve and its mechanistic locus would change fine-tuning practice and support alignment-preserving adaptation methods.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Forgetting is well known, but the breadth-versus-domain trade-off curve for open-vocabulary detection, with mechanistic localization to alignment components, may be uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune public open-vocabulary detectors on domain datasets, evaluate both broad and domain vocabularies at dense checkpoints, and run layer-wise probes to localize forgetting.
main_risk: Results depend on fine-tuning hyperparameters, so the study needs a hyperparameter envelope rather than one recipe to support general claims.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Light domain fine-tuning is assumed to add domain skill while roughly preserving pretraining capabilities.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The alignment mapping is low-dimensional and shared across all vocabulary, so narrow-class gradients distort it globally, unlike the redundant visual features behind it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one detector on one small domain set, evaluate the original benchmark vocabulary at three checkpoints, and plot the two curves in a short run.

one_line_idea: State breaks detectors before category does: foundation detectors fail on known objects in unusual states, overturned, disassembled, damaged, more than on unseen categories in canonical states.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generalization discussions in detection are organized around category novelty, while deployment failures often involve familiar categories in unfamiliar physical states, and web imagery over-represents intact, canonical object states.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The effective generalization frontier of foundation detectors is state-space, not category-space, so detection of common categories in atypical states is worse than detection of rare categories in typical states, inverting the field's implicit difficulty ordering and revealing state coverage as the binding constraint.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A matched comparison, common categories in atypical states versus benchmark-rare categories in typical states, will show lower recall on the former for foundation detectors, with errors dominated by missed detection rather than mislabeling.
why_important: Safety-critical detection, accidents, damage, disassembly, is precisely the atypical-state regime, and a category-centric research agenda leaves this axis unmeasured and unimproved.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] State-based generalization exists in cognitive-science-flavored work, but a quantitative state-versus-category difficulty inversion for detection foundation models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate atypical-state imagery for common categories and typical-state imagery for rare categories, match on visual difficulty proxies, and compare recall across the two conditions for several detectors.
main_risk: Matching difficulty across the two conditions is the crux, requiring careful control for size, occlusion, and image quality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Category novelty is treated as the hard generalization axis, with within-category variation assumed handled by data diversity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web data covers many categories but samples each near its canonical state, so state diversity per category is far poorer than category diversity, making state the thin direction of the training distribution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Collect a few dozen images of overturned or disassembled common objects, run one foundation detector, and compare recall against its rare-category performance in a day.

one_line_idea: Foundation detectors cannot say this image is not for me: on out-of-scope imagery they emit confident structured detections instead of abstaining, and no standard evaluation measures scope awareness.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detectors are applied to whatever images arrive in a pipeline, including out-of-scope inputs like documents, rendered interfaces, or non-photographic sensor data, and detection benchmarks contain only in-scope imagery.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation detectors produce confident, plausible-looking detection sets on radically out-of-scope inputs at rates similar to in-scope imagery, their score distributions carry almost no signal usable for scope rejection, and this scope blindness is invariant to model scale, defining a missing capability orthogonal to accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring detection-count and confidence distributions on out-of-scope image suites will show heavy overlap with in-scope statistics, and scope classification from detector outputs alone will perform far worse than a trivial dedicated scope classifier, across model scales.
why_important: Automated pipelines act on detections without human review, and confident nonsense on out-of-scope inputs is a silent integrity failure that scale, the field's default remedy, does not fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Out-of-distribution detection is studied for classification, and a scope-awareness evaluation designed around structured detection outputs may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble out-of-scope suites spanning document, synthetic, and non-photographic imagery, characterize detector output statistics against in-scope baselines, and benchmark scope rejection from detector signals versus a small dedicated classifier.
main_risk: Defining out-of-scope precisely is subtle, since some pipelines legitimately expect detectors to work on renders or documents, so scope definitions must be application-anchored.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Low confidence is assumed to naturally accompany inputs a model cannot handle.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confidence heads are trained only on in-scope data, so their behavior off-scope is an unconstrained extrapolation with no reason to be low.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run one foundation detector on a few hundred documents and rendered screenshots and summarize the confident-detection statistics in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: At foundation scale, detection error is almost all recognition: class-agnostic localization is near ceiling, so architecture work on box mechanisms attacks a solved subproblem.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection improvements are reported as aggregate AP, and the community continues to invest heavily in localization machinery, proposal mechanisms, box refinement, and matching schemes, without routinely decomposing remaining error into localization versus recognition components.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For modern large-backbone detectors, class-agnostic recall at moderate IoU with realistic proposal budgets is close to its ceiling on standard benchmarks, the overwhelming majority of residual AP loss traces to classification and scoring errors, and this recognition share has grown monotonically with backbone scale, implying localization-focused research now yields structurally diminishing returns.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] An error-decomposition audit across detector generations will show the recognition-attributable share of residual error growing with scale and dominating for current models, and oracle-classification interventions will recover several times more AP than oracle-localization interventions.
why_important: Research portfolio allocation follows perceived bottlenecks; establishing that recognition dominates residual error would redirect effort toward classification, scoring, and naming interfaces rather than box machinery.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Error-decomposition tools exist, but a scale-trend analysis showing localization saturating and recognition becoming the binding constraint across model generations may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply a fixed decomposition protocol with oracle substitutions across a spectrum of public detectors ordered by scale and plot the attribution shares against scale.
main_risk: Decomposition results depend on protocol choices such as oracle ordering, so multiple decomposition conventions must agree for the conclusion to stand.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Localization and recognition are treated as comparably open subproblems, with box machinery innovation seen as a live path to headline gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectness and box geometry are low-entropy, category-generic structures that big backbones learn easily, while fine-grained naming across a large vocabulary retains irreducible confusability that scale attacks much more slowly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one current strong detector, compare AP recovered by oracle labels on its boxes versus oracle boxes with its labels, one afternoon with cached predictions.

one_line_idea: Localization and recognition want incompatible features: two-stream detectors reading separate frozen representations for where and what beat single-feature detectors at matched compute.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard detectors compute both localization and classification from one shared feature map, and the two subtasks impose conflicting invariance demands, spatial equivariance and precision for boxes, appearance invariance and semantic abstraction for labels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The shared-feature compromise measurably hurts both subtasks, so routing localization and recognition heads to separately optimized representations, one geometry-preserving, one semantics-preserving, outperforms shared-feature detectors at matched total compute, with the gain concentrated where the two demands conflict most, small objects and fine-grained classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Controlled comparisons of shared versus split representations at matched compute will show the split variant ahead, with interaction effects, geometry stream mattering for high-IoU metrics, semantic stream for fine-grained accuracy, confirming the conflict diagnosis.
why_important: If the shared-backbone dogma costs performance, detector design and foundation-model interface design should expose multiple representation taps rather than one, changing how backbones are built and served.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Decoupled heads are common, but decoupled representations sourced from differently optimized encoders under matched-compute discipline may be untested as a clean hypothesis.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched-compute detector variants reading shared versus split frozen encoders, evaluate with subtask-resolved metrics, and test the predicted interaction pattern.
main_risk: Matched-compute accounting across one large versus two small encoders is delicate and drives the conclusion, requiring transparent budget definitions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A single strong backbone is assumed to serve both subtasks adequately, with head-level decoupling considered sufficient.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A representation cannot simultaneously maximize invariance and equivariance to the same transformations, so any single feature map sits on a Pareto frontier between the two subtasks' needs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Feed an existing detector's localization head from an earlier layer and its classifier from a later layer of the same frozen backbone and check for subtask-resolved movement in a quick retrain of heads only.

one_line_idea: IoU-threshold sweeps fingerprint what a method actually improved: most claimed detection advances are either pure-recognition or pure-localization gains, and the sweep signature exposes mislabeled contributions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Headline AP averages over IoU thresholds, so a gain concentrated at low thresholds, better recognition and ranking, and a gain concentrated at high thresholds, better box precision, produce identical headline movement while being entirely different contributions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Classifying published methods by their AP-versus-IoU-threshold gain profiles yields a clean two-cluster structure, recognition-type and localization-type, the claimed mechanisms of a nontrivial fraction of methods mismatch their measured cluster, and the profile predicts transfer, recognition-type gains transfer across box conventions while localization-type gains do not.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Threshold-resolved re-evaluation of reproducible methods against their baselines will show most gains strongly concentrated at one end, mechanism-claim mismatches in a measurable fraction, and profile-predicted transfer behavior across evaluation conventions.
why_important: Understanding what a method actually improved determines when to adopt it, and a cheap diagnostic fingerprint would raise the evidentiary standard for mechanism claims across detection papers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Threshold-resolved reporting exists, but systematic profiling of the literature's claimed-versus-measured contribution types may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reproduce a set of methods with public code, compute gain profiles over IoU thresholds against shared baselines, cluster the profiles, and audit mechanism claims against cluster membership.
main_risk: Reproduction fidelity limits the audit, so the method set must be restricted to well-documented public implementations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Headline AP gains are read as broad detection improvement consistent with whatever mechanism the paper narrates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The averaged metric was designed for summary, not diagnosis, and its components carry cleanly separable information that reporting culture happens to discard.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Recompute threshold-resolved gains for three methods with cached predictions and check whether each concentrates at one end of the threshold range.

one_line_idea: Detectors should output box uncertainty, not just label confidence: cheap per-coordinate uncertainty adds little AP but transforms downstream decision quality, exposing a metric-deployment mismatch.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection outputs carry one scalar confidence conflating existence, label, and localization quality, while downstream consumers, trackers, planners, measurement systems, need to know specifically how trustworthy the box geometry is.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-coordinate localization uncertainty estimated by lightweight heads is well correlated with realized box error, propagating it to downstream tasks improves their decisions substantially even though detection AP barely moves, and the field's AP monoculture is why such outputs remain nonstandard despite negligible cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Adding a calibrated box-uncertainty head to standard detectors will leave AP within noise while improving downstream proxies, tracking association quality, measurement error bounds, fusion accuracy, by margins larger than typical between-detector AP gaps.
why_important: If a near-free output channel dominates AP-visible differences for downstream value, evaluation and interface conventions, not modeling, are the bottleneck, which is a correctable community-level failure.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Box-uncertainty heads exist in the literature, but the deployment-value-versus-AP-invisibility argument, quantified across downstream tasks, may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train uncertainty-headed variants of standard detectors, verify calibration of coordinate uncertainties, and run matched downstream evaluations with and without uncertainty propagation.
main_risk: Downstream gains depend on consumers designed to exploit uncertainty, so the study must include realistic consumer implementations rather than strawmen.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The scalar confidence score is treated as a sufficient uncertainty interface for detection outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A single scalar cannot express that a box is certainly the right object but has an unreliable bottom edge, and downstream geometry consumers need exactly that distinction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train a small box-uncertainty head on a frozen detector, check coordinate-error correlation, and plug it into one public tracker in a short engineering sprint.

one_line_idea: Extent errors, not center errors, dominate the high-IoU regime, and they trace to annotation-convention ambiguity about what counts as the object, handles, shadows, occluded parts, rather than to model weakness.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] High-IoU localization quality has become a differentiator among strong detectors, and box annotation guidelines leave genuinely ambiguous decisions, attached parts, transparent regions, occlusion completion, to annotator discretion.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Decomposing localization error into center displacement and extent mismatch will show extent dominating at high IoU, extent errors will concentrate on objects with convention-ambiguous parts, and model extent predictions will track dataset-specific annotation conventions, meaning the high-IoU race partly measures convention fitting rather than geometric perception.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Error decomposition across detectors will attribute most high-IoU failures to extent, ambiguity-flagged objects will show several times higher extent error, and cross-dataset evaluation will reveal systematic extent shifts matching known convention differences.
why_important: If high-IoU differences reflect convention fitting, cross-dataset high-IoU comparisons are invalid, and progress claims in the precision regime need convention-controlled evaluation to mean anything.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Localization error analyses exist, but tying the extent-error dominance to annotation-convention ambiguity with cross-dataset convention signatures may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a center-versus-extent decomposition, annotate ambiguity flags on a benchmark sample, evaluate several detectors, and run cross-dataset extent-shift analysis on convention-differing datasets.
main_risk: Ambiguity flagging is itself subjective, requiring multiple annotators and agreement reporting to ground the analysis.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] High-IoU AP differences are read as differences in models' geometric precision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where the object ends is partly a definitional question, and no model can be geometrically right about a boundary that annotation conventions themselves place inconsistently.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Decompose high-IoU failures of one detector into center versus extent components from cached predictions and inspect the ambiguous-part concentration in one session.

one_line_idea: Detection classification is not crop classification: region labels depend on an optimal, class-specific amount of context, and both context-free crops and whole-image reasoning underperform the learned intermediate.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] It is tempting to treat detection classification as image classification on crops, reusing powerful image-level foundation classifiers, and detectors internally pool features from receptive fields larger than the box.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Classification accuracy on ground-truth boxes as a function of included context around the crop follows an inverted-U with a class-dependent optimum, strong image-level classifiers applied to tight crops lose substantially to detector-internal classification, and the optimal context ratio is predictable from class properties like size, context dependence, and confusability.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping context margins for crop-based classification with a strong foundation classifier will show the inverted-U with optima varying across classes, and even the per-class-optimal crop pipeline will trail detector-internal classification on cluttered scenes.
why_important: The result would explain why bolting foundation classifiers onto proposals underperforms, quantify what detector heads add, and provide design guidance for retrieval-augmented or classifier-augmented detection systems.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context effects on recognition are classical, but a quantitative context-optimum characterization for modern foundation classifiers in the detection loop may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate crop-margin sweeps with public foundation classifiers on oracle boxes across a benchmark, fit per-class optima, and compare against the classification accuracy of detectors' own heads on identical boxes.
main_risk: Crop resizing interacts with resolution effects, so margin sweeps must control effective object resolution to isolate context contribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A strong enough image classifier on a decent crop is assumed to solve region classification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Region identity in cluttered scenes is partly determined by relations to surroundings, which tight crops discard and whole images drown, so an intermediate context level must be optimal and its position class-dependent.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a foundation classifier on oracle boxes at three context margins for one benchmark subset and compare against the detector's own labels in a day.

one_line_idea: Objectness saturates early while recognition keeps scaling: detection-specific pretraining spends compute on a subskill that stops improving, arguing for classification-heavy pretraining plus minimal localization adaptation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection-oriented pretraining pipelines allocate large compute to localization-bearing objectives, and scaling studies report aggregate transfer numbers without decomposing which detection subskills actually improve with scale.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Class-agnostic localization ability extracted from pretrained models saturates at modest scale and data, while region-recognition ability continues improving over the same scaling range, so compute reallocated from localization-heavy to recognition-heavy pretraining, with a small localization adapter, yields better detectors at fixed budget.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Subskill-decomposed probing across a pretraining scale ladder will show flat objectness curves beyond an early point and rising recognition curves, and budget-matched recipes weighted toward recognition pretraining will win on final detection metrics.
why_important: Pretraining budgets are the dominant cost in the foundation era, and knowing which detection subskill scaling actually buys would restructure how detection foundation models are trained.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scaling analyses of detection transfer exist in aggregate, but subskill-resolved saturation curves with a budget-reallocation consequence may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe objectness and recognition separately across public checkpoints of different scales, then train budget-matched detectors from recipes differing in objective mix to test the reallocation prediction.
main_risk: Probing methodology can under-measure latent abilities, so multiple probe designs are needed before declaring a subskill saturated.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More detection-flavored pretraining is assumed better, with all subskills benefiting from scale together.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectness is a low-complexity, high-regularity target that small models fit quickly, while open-set recognition has effectively unbounded complexity, so their scaling curves should diverge by basic learning-theory intuition.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe class-agnostic proposal recall on three checkpoints of one model family spanning scale and check for early flattening in one evaluation pass.

one_line_idea: Duplicate suppression is a recognition problem misassigned to geometry: identity-aware deduplication that asks are these the same object beats overlap-threshold suppression exactly where detection is hardest, adjacent identical objects.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deduplication in detectors is performed by geometric overlap rules or learned modules trained with geometric supervision, and adjacent identical objects produce true boxes with overlap statistics indistinguishable from duplicate predictions of one object.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The information that distinguishes two adjacent instances from duplicate hypotheses of one instance is appearance-level instance identity, invisible to geometry, so suppression informed by an instance-identity signal, learned from appearance correspondence, dominates geometric suppression on dense same-class scenes at equal budgets, while matching it elsewhere.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On dense same-class benchmarks, identity-aware suppression will simultaneously reduce duplicate false positives and merged-neighbor misses relative to tuned geometric suppression, with the advantage growing with instance density and shrinking to zero on sparse scenes.
why_important: Suppression is the last untouched geometric heuristic in otherwise learned pipelines, and dense same-class scenes, retail, biology, agriculture, crowds, are major application domains bottlenecked exactly there.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Learned suppression exists, but framing deduplication as instance-identity recognition with appearance correspondence supervision may be an unoccupied design point.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement identity-aware suppression atop existing detectors using an appearance-similarity module, evaluate against tuned geometric and learned-geometric suppression on density-stratified benchmarks, and verify the predicted density interaction.
main_risk: Identical products or organisms may genuinely lack distinguishing appearance, capping identity signals precisely where they are most needed, which the experiment itself would quantify.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Suppression is treated as a solved plumbing detail handled adequately by overlap thresholds or their learned equivalents.
why_it_might_be_wrong: No function of box geometry alone can separate the two hypotheses when overlap distributions coincide, so the ceiling of geometric suppression on dense scenes is a mathematical fact, not an engineering gap.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one dense dataset, measure how often tuned geometric suppression's errors involve adjacent same-class instances versus true duplicates, quantifying the addressable error mass in one analysis session.

one_line_idea: A scene-statistics decision rule for counting: measurable image properties predict whether detection-based or regression-based counting will be more accurate on a given image, enabling per-image method routing.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Counting systems choose between detection-based and density-regression approaches globally per application, and real workloads mix sparse and dense images whose optimal method differs image by image.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cheap per-image statistics, estimated density, size distribution, overlap structure, predict the sign of the accuracy difference between the two counting paradigms reliably enough that a learned router choosing per image beats either paradigm applied uniformly, by a margin that grows with workload heterogeneity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A router trained on scene statistics will select the better paradigm on a strong majority of held-out images, and routed counting error will undercut the best single-paradigm error across mixed workloads.
why_important: Counting underlies inventory, ecology, and crowd safety, and a validated routing rule converts an either-or architectural debate into a measurable, deployable decision procedure.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Method-selection meta-learning exists elsewhere, but a scene-statistics router for the detection-versus-density counting choice may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate both paradigms per image on datasets spanning densities, train a router on simple statistics, and compare routed error against uniform-paradigm baselines on held-out workload mixes.
main_risk: The router's own feature extraction could be as expensive as running both methods, so the statistics must be genuinely cheap or shared with the counting pipeline.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Counting method choice is treated as a per-application architecture decision settled by domain convention.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The failure regimes of the two paradigms are governed by observable geometry, suppression collapse under overlap for detection, calibration drift in sparse scenes for regression, so the optimal choice is predictable from that geometry.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one mixed-density dataset, evaluate both paradigms per image and check how often a two-feature threshold rule picks the winner, one analysis afternoon.

one_line_idea: Multimodal LLM counting is subitizing plus guessing: exact counting holds up to a small integer and then collapses to density-conditioned estimation, a signature invisible in benchmarks that average over count ranges.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal language models are marketed as able to count objects in images, and counting benchmarks typically report a single aggregate accuracy over images whose true counts span a wide range.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model counting behavior decomposes into two regimes, near-exact performance up to a small threshold and coarse magnitude estimation beyond it, with errors in the second regime scaling with the true count and correlating with density cues rather than enumeration, so aggregate benchmark scores mask a qualitative capability boundary.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Count-resolved evaluation will show a sharp accuracy cliff at a small count threshold consistent across models, beyond which error distributions match magnitude-estimation signatures, roughly multiplicative errors, rather than enumeration signatures, occasional off-by-small-integer errors.
why_important: Downstream users treat model counts as enumeration; if large counts are density guesses, applications from inventory to reporting inherit silent multiplicative errors, and benchmark aggregates fail to warn them.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Subitizing-like behavior has been speculated for multimodal models, and a rigorous two-regime characterization with error-signature analysis may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build count-controlled image sets spanning exact small counts through large crowds, evaluate several multimodal models, and fit two-regime models to the error structure per model.
main_risk: Confounding between count and visual clutter must be controlled by holding object type and layout statistics fixed across count levels.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Counting accuracy is treated as a smooth capability improving with model scale, adequately summarized by one benchmark number.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Exact enumeration requires serial attention-like binding that feedforward vision-language interfaces may not implement, while density estimation is learnable from image statistics, naturally producing the two-regime split.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Photograph controlled arrangements from two to a hundred identical objects, query one model, and plot error against true count in a day.

one_line_idea: Crowding suppresses per-instance recall independent of resolution: detection probability of an instance declines with the number of identical neighbors even when size and image quality are held constant.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense-scene performance is usually explained through small object size and occlusion, and evaluation rarely isolates the effect of instance multiplicity itself at fixed size and visibility.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detectors exhibit a crowding effect analogous to the one documented in human peripheral vision, per-instance recall falls as identical-instance count rises even with size, spacing, and visibility controlled, driven by suppression machinery and by feature interference among similar neighbors rather than by pixel-level information limits.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On synthetic and photographed arrays where instance size and visibility are held constant while count varies, per-instance recall will decline measurably with count, and the decline will persist after replacing suppression with oracle deduplication, isolating a feature-level interference component.
why_important: If multiplicity itself degrades detection, dense-scene applications face a previously unquantified error source, and the standard size-and-occlusion explanation of dense-scene difficulty is incomplete.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Crowding is a classic perception phenomenon, and a controlled multiplicity-isolated measurement for machine detectors with a suppression-versus-features decomposition may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct count-controlled arrays with fixed instance size and spacing, evaluate several detectors with standard and oracle deduplication, and fit recall as a function of count under each condition.
main_risk: Perfectly controlling visibility and local contrast across counts is delicate, and residual low-level confounds could mimic a multiplicity effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-instance detection difficulty is assumed to depend on the instance's own appearance and visibility, not on how many similar instances share the scene.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both suppression rules and locally pooled features couple nearby similar objects, so the independence assumption is architecturally false and only awaits quantification.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Photograph fixed-size object arrays at several counts, run one detector, and plot per-instance recall against count in a day.

one_line_idea: Counts are cheap detection supervision: adding per-image count labels for classes without box annotations improves detection of those classes, unlocking abundant inventory-style metadata as training signal.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many operational datasets carry per-image counts from inventories, logs, or reports without any box annotation, and detection training pipelines currently have no standard way to consume count-only labels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Count labels constrain detector outputs strongly enough, through a differentiable counting consistency loss on predicted detections, to improve AP for count-supervised classes over both box-only baselines and image-level-tag weak supervision, because counts carry instance-multiplicity information that presence tags lack.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Mixed-supervision training, boxes for some classes and counts only for others, will improve AP on the count-only classes over tag-only weak supervision at matched data, with the gain increasing for classes that frequently appear in multiples.
why_important: Count metadata already exists at industrial scale for retail, agriculture, and logistics, so validating counts as detection supervision would unlock large training resources at zero annotation cost.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weakly supervised detection from tags is established, and systematic use of exact counts as the weak signal, with an analysis of when counts beat tags, may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate count-only supervision by stripping boxes from selected classes of a standard dataset, train with a counting consistency objective, and compare against tag-supervised and box-supervised references.
main_risk: Counting losses over discrete detections require relaxations whose gradients may be unstable, making the negative result attributable to optimization rather than information content.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Weak supervision for detection is mentally equated with image-level presence tags, with counts not treated as a distinct richer signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A count pins down the exact number of instances the detector must produce, eliminating the degenerate solutions that plague presence-tag supervision, such as firing once on the most salient instance.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Strip boxes from three multi-instance classes, train with a simple soft-count penalty, and check for AP movement against a tag-supervised control in a short training cycle.

one_line_idea: Detector-regressor disagreement finds annotation errors: images where detection-based and density-based counts diverge are enriched for ground-truth mistakes, yielding a free annotation-audit signal.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Counting datasets contain annotation errors, missed instances, double marks, and boundary-case judgment calls, and auditing annotations at scale is expensive and unguided.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detection-based and density-based counters fail in nearly uncorrelated ways on model-difficult images but agree with each other when the annotation is wrong and the image is easy, so ranking images by paradigm disagreement with the annotation, conditioned on paradigm agreement with each other, concentrates annotation errors far above base rate, enabling targeted re-annotation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Human auditing of images where both paradigms agree with each other but disagree with the label will find annotation-error rates several times the dataset base rate, while images where paradigms disagree with each other will be enriched for genuine visual difficulty instead.
why_important: A cheap, automatic triage signal for annotation quality would improve datasets across counting and detection, and the agreement-conditioned design generalizes to other task pairs with complementary failure modes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Model-disagreement-based label auditing exists for classification, and the cross-paradigm agreement-conditioned variant for counting and detection annotation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run both paradigms on annotated counting datasets, stratify images by the agreement structure among the two models and the label, sample strata for expert re-annotation, and measure error enrichment per stratum.
main_risk: If the two paradigms share failure modes on specific scene types, their agreement stops indicating label error there, weakening the triage in exactly those regions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Annotation auditing is treated as requiring either exhaustive human passes or single-model confidence heuristics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Two systems with different inductive biases agreeing against the label is statistical evidence about the label, and the conditioning cleanly separates label suspicion from image difficulty.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one public counting dataset, rank images by the agreement-conditioned disagreement score and manually inspect the top fifty for label errors in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Partial-visibility conventions drive counting disagreement: a large share of counting error concentrates on instances whose countability is convention-ambiguous, edge-cropped, mostly occluded, or reflected objects.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Datasets differ and are internally inconsistent in whether barely visible instances, edge-cropped objects, reflections, and depictions count as instances, and counting metrics charge all disagreement to the model.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Stratifying counting and detection errors by an instance-countability ambiguity score will show model error concentrating heavily on convention-ambiguous instances, models trained on different datasets will disagree with each other primarily on those same instances, and re-scoring with ambiguity-aware tolerance will substantially shrink both measured error and cross-dataset transfer gaps.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Errors on unambiguous instances will be a minority of total counting error for strong models, and cross-dataset performance drops will be disproportionately explained by the ambiguous stratum rather than by distribution shift on clear instances.
why_important: If convention ambiguity dominates residual error, further model improvement is misdirected, and the field needs annotation-standard reform and ambiguity-aware metrics more than new architectures.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotation ambiguity is acknowledged anecdotally, and a quantitative attribution of counting and detection residual error to countability conventions may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define an ambiguity rubric, have annotators flag ambiguous instances on evaluation subsets, and recompute model errors and cross-dataset gaps with stratified and tolerance-based scoring.
main_risk: The ambiguity rubric could circularly absorb model errors if designed post hoc, so it must be fixed from annotation-guideline analysis before seeing model outputs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Residual counting error is read as perceptual failure that better models will eliminate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: When ground truth itself is convention-dependent, part of any model-label disagreement is definitional rather than perceptual, and that part cannot be modeled away.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Manually flag ambiguous instances in a few hundred evaluation images and measure what fraction of one model's counting error lands on them.

one_line_idea: Class-averaged detection AP is driven by a volatile minority: bootstrap analysis shows overall benchmark rankings hinge on a handful of high-variance classes, making leaderboard stability an illusion.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark AP averages per-class AP with equal weights while classes differ enormously in test instance counts, so classes with few instances contribute high-variance terms to the headline number.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The variance of headline AP is concentrated in a small set of low-instance-count classes, method rankings frequently reorder under test-set resampling because of exactly those classes, and reporting AP with class-stratified uncertainty or trimmed aggregation would change which methods appear to lead on established benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Image-level bootstrap of standard benchmark evaluation will show a small class subset accounting for most headline-AP variance, and pairwise method comparisons with small reported gaps will flip in a nontrivial fraction of bootstrap replicates.
why_important: The field's progress narrative is built on small headline-AP deltas, and if those deltas are dominated by a few noisy classes, method selection and research direction are being steered by statistical noise.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Statistical instability of AP has been noted in principle, but a variance-decomposition identifying the volatile-class structure and its effect on leaderboard order may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap evaluation for a pool of public detectors with cached predictions, decompose headline-AP variance by class, and quantify ranking flip rates as a function of reported gap size.
main_risk: Bootstrap over images approximates but does not equal fresh-data variance, so conclusions should be framed as lower bounds on instability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Headline AP differences of a fraction of a point on major benchmarks are routinely treated as real method differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Equal class weighting amplifies the noisiest terms of the average, an elementary variance effect that per-class instance-count disparities make severe.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap two methods with similar reported AP from cached predictions and count ranking flips across replicates in one session.

one_line_idea: AP rewards unusable predictions: methods gain benchmark points from dense low-confidence box floods that no deployment threshold would keep, so operating-point metrics reorder detection leaderboards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] AP integrates precision over the full recall range including regions reachable only at very low confidence thresholds, and deployed systems operate at high-precision thresholds where most of those predictions are discarded.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable share of between-method AP differences on standard benchmarks comes from the low-confidence tail that deployment never uses, so ranking methods by fixed-false-positive-rate operating metrics changes their order, and some celebrated methods derive most of their advantage from tail-region behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Recomputing method comparisons under operating-point metrics, recall at fixed false positives per image, will show ranking divergence from AP, with the divergence attributable to the sub-threshold score region by decomposition of the precision-recall curves.
why_important: If leaderboard advantages live below deployable thresholds, the community optimizes and publishes improvements users can never realize, a systematic misallocation of research signal.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The critique of full-curve integration is old, but a quantified attribution of modern method gaps to the unusable score region may be undone for current detectors.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-score public detector pools under a family of operating-point metrics, decompose AP gaps by score region, and identify methods whose advantages concentrate below practical thresholds.
main_risk: The definition of a practical threshold is application-dependent, so a range of operating points must be reported rather than one arbitrary choice.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] AP is treated as a neutral summary whose improvements translate proportionally to deployed performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Integrating over all thresholds weights curve regions by mathematical convention rather than by use, and nothing forces the low-threshold region to correlate with the high-precision region across methods.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For three public methods, compare AP ranking against recall at one false positive per image from cached predictions in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Evaluation-implementation drift silently moves detection scores: subtle differences among popular evaluation toolkits in crowd handling, area computation, and tie-breaking are large enough to flip close method comparisons.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multiple evaluation implementations coexist across frameworks and papers, and they encode small independent decisions about ignore regions, degenerate boxes, duplicate resolution, and rounding that are rarely documented in publications.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-toolkit score differences for identical predictions are of comparable magnitude to typical published method gaps, the differences are systematic rather than random, penalizing specific prediction styles, and some cross-paper comparisons in the literature mix toolkits in ways that could reverse their conclusions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Feeding identical prediction files through the popular evaluation implementations will produce per-method score spreads on the order of typical leaderboard gaps, with the spread differing by method in a way that changes at least some pairwise orderings.
why_important: Comparability of published numbers is the foundation of empirical progress claims, and unquantified toolkit drift undermines that foundation at the scale where most claimed improvements live.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anecdotes about toolkit differences circulate, and a systematic cross-toolkit audit with method-dependent bias analysis may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect cached predictions from a method pool, evaluate each through the major toolkits under nominally identical settings, and characterize the size, systematicity, and ranking impact of the discrepancies.
main_risk: Toolkits differ partly by declared configuration rather than hidden behavior, so the audit must carefully separate documented setting differences from silent implementation drift.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Evaluation code is assumed interchangeable, with reported metric names taken as sufficient specification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: AP computation involves dozens of micro-decisions that standards documents do not pin down, and independent implementations resolve them independently, guaranteeing drift somewhere.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run one prediction file through three evaluation implementations and diff the outputs, an afternoon of plumbing.

one_line_idea: Detection test sets are effectively smaller than they look: image-level and instance-level near-duplicates inflate effective sample size, understating uncertainty and overstating fine-grained method distinctions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Large detection test sets were assembled from web sources with limited dedup tooling at collection time, and statistical treatment of evaluation assumes approximately independent test units.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard detection test sets contain enough near-duplicate imagery, repeated scenes, burst frames, recropped versions, that the effective independent sample size is substantially below the nominal count, so all uncertainty estimates are optimistic and some reported method distinctions fall inside the corrected noise floor.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Modern embedding-based near-duplicate mining on standard detection test sets will identify a meaningful duplicate fraction, and recomputing evaluation with duplicate-cluster-aware resampling will widen confidence intervals enough to erase some published-scale gaps.
why_important: Every significance claim on these benchmarks inherits the independence assumption, so quantifying its violation recalibrates the evidential weight of a large body of results.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Duplicate analyses exist for classification training sets, and a duplication-aware statistical correction for detection evaluation sets may be unperformed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine near-duplicates on major detection test sets with embedding similarity plus human verification, form duplicate clusters, and re-evaluate method pools with cluster-level bootstrap.
main_risk: Near-duplicate is a threshold-dependent notion, so results must be reported across similarity thresholds with human-validated calibration.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Test-set size in images is treated as the effective sample size for judging the reliability of benchmark differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web-collected imagery is heavy-tailed in scene popularity, and popular scenes recur across sources, making some duplication a statistical certainty rather than a possibility.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run embedding-based duplicate mining on one benchmark test set and manually verify the top few hundred candidate pairs in a day.

one_line_idea: The default detection-count cap censors dense scenes: standard evaluation truncates predictions per image at a fixed limit, so performance on the densest images is systematically unmeasured and methods are blind-ranked there.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard evaluation protocols cap the number of scored detections per image, and some benchmark images contain more ground-truth instances than the cap allows predictions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The prediction cap materially censors evaluation on high-instance-count images, methods differing specifically in dense-scene ability receive nearly identical scores because their differences are truncated away, and uncapped or density-scaled evaluation would reorder methods for dense-scene applications.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Recomputing evaluation with raised caps will leave sparse-image scores unchanged while measurably changing dense-image scores and their method ordering, demonstrating that the standard protocol cannot see dense-scene differences.
why_important: Users select detectors for crowd, retail, and aerial workloads using benchmark numbers that are provably insensitive to exactly their regime, a concrete and fixable evaluation blind spot.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The cap is documented as a protocol constant, but its censoring effect on dense-scene method comparison may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate public method pools under a sweep of detection caps, stratify by ground-truth instance count, and measure where scores and rankings become cap-sensitive.
main_risk: Raising caps rewards prediction flooding unless paired with operating-point analysis, so the corrected protocol needs joint design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The evaluation cap is regarded as a harmless computational convenience with no effect on scientific conclusions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On an image whose instance count exceeds the cap, recall above the cap ratio is mathematically unreachable, so the metric is censored by construction and dense-scene ability cannot register.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score two methods on the densest decile of one benchmark with a raised cap and compare against capped scores in one session.

one_line_idea: Greedy confidence-ordered matching biases AP against certain prediction styles: optimal-assignment scoring changes per-method AP unevenly, revealing that part of measured differences is matching-algorithm artifact.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard AP matches predictions to ground truth greedily in confidence order, and greedy matching is not optimal assignment, so the scored match structure depends on confidence ordering even for identical box sets.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Methods whose confidence ranking correlates differently with localization quality are penalized differently by greedy matching, so re-scoring with optimal bipartite assignment shifts per-method AP unevenly, and some between-method gaps shrink or reverse, exposing a matching-rule component inside reported differences.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Optimal-assignment re-scoring of cached predictions will change AP by method-dependent amounts, largest for methods with miscalibrated confidence-versus-IoU relationships, and at least some close leaderboard orderings will flip.
why_important: If the matching algorithm contributes to method differences, conclusions about model quality contain an arbitrary protocol component that a better-founded scoring rule would remove.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Matching-rule sensitivity of detection metrics may be folklore among evaluation implementers, but a quantified method-bias analysis appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement optimal-assignment scoring, re-score a public method pool on standard benchmarks, and analyze which prediction-style properties predict per-method score movement.
main_risk: Optimal assignment has its own debatable design freedoms, such as the objective weighting between IoU and confidence, requiring several variants for robustness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The greedy matching rule is treated as a definitional constant of AP rather than a choice with method-dependent consequences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Greedy algorithms are order-sensitive by nature, and confidence order is a model output, so the protocol couples scoring to a model property unrelated to detection correctness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score two stylistically different methods, one query-based and one dense, under greedy versus optimal matching from cached predictions in a day.

one_line_idea: Unreported inference-time enhancements account for a large share of detection leaderboard deltas: equal-inference-budget re-evaluation collapses many claimed architecture advantages.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection results are reported with heterogeneous and inconsistently disclosed inference-time settings, input resolutions, multi-scale testing, flipping, ensemble-like augmentation, and these settings change scores substantially.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Normalizing a representative slice of claimed method improvements to matched inference compute and identical test-time settings will eliminate or reverse a substantial fraction of the deltas, showing that a nontrivial part of perceived architectural progress is unstandardized inference-time expenditure.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under a fixed inference-budget protocol, the distribution of method-over-baseline deltas will shift markedly toward zero relative to originally reported deltas, with some prominent orderings inverting.
why_important: If progress partly reflects inference-budget inflation, the field's architecture narrative is distorted and efficiency-adjusted evaluation should become the reporting standard.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compute-matched comparisons are advocated in principle, but a systematic re-evaluation quantifying the test-time-settings share of detection progress may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select reproducible methods spanning several years, re-evaluate all under one fixed inference budget and settings profile, and compare normalized deltas against reported deltas.
main_risk: Some methods are architecturally entangled with specific inference procedures, making a fair common protocol genuinely hard to define for them.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported gains are attributed to modeling contributions, with test-time settings assumed comparable across papers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Test-time enhancements are cheap score levers with inconsistent disclosure norms, and any inconsistently applied lever inflates the apparent variance of modeling quality.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take two methods with claimed gaps, equalize resolution and disable test-time augmentation for both, and re-measure the gap in one session.

one_line_idea: Corruption-suite robustness does not predict natural-shift robustness for detection: model rankings on synthetic corruptions and on natural distribution shifts are close to uncorrelated.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection robustness is commonly certified with synthetic corruption suites, while deployment failures arise from natural shifts, new geographies, times, sensors, and scene compositions, and the two shift families have different statistical structure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across a diverse detector pool, corruption-suite robustness scores explain little of the variance in natural-shift robustness, methods tuned for corruption performance gain nothing or negative amounts on natural shifts, so corruption benchmarks function as a misleading proxy in detection model selection.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Correlating relative performance drops across a matrix of detectors, synthetic corruption suites, and natural-shift test sets will show weak cross-family correlation after controlling for clean accuracy, with some corruption-optimized models among the worst under natural shift.
why_important: Robustness claims drive deployment decisions in safety-relevant domains, and a broken proxy channels engineering effort into hardening against shifts that do not occur while ignoring ones that do.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Proxy failure between synthetic and natural robustness has been studied for classification, and the detection-specific version with its localization-error structure may be unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble matched clean, corrupted, and naturally shifted evaluation sets for detection, evaluate a broad model pool, and analyze cross-family rank correlations of robustness with clean-performance partialing.
main_risk: Natural-shift test sets differ from clean sets in annotation protocol as well as distribution, so annotation-consistency controls are needed before attributing drops to shift.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Corruption-suite scores are treated as general-purpose robustness certificates for detection models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synthetic corruptions perturb pixels while natural shifts perturb scene generation, and invariances to the former say nothing structural about the latter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For an existing detector pool with published corruption scores, evaluate on one natural-shift set and compute the rank correlation in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Benchmark precision is annotation-limited for top detectors: a substantial share of their scored false positives are correct detections of unannotated objects, so measured precision differences among strong models are annotation artifacts.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection ground truth misses instances due to annotator fatigue, ambiguity, and protocol limits, and evaluation charges every unmatched prediction as a false positive regardless of whether the object is really there.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For current strong detectors on standard benchmarks, the fraction of scored false positives that are actually correct detections of unannotated objects is large enough that measured precision saturates against the annotation rather than against model ability, and between-model precision differences at the top of leaderboards mostly reflect differential alignment with annotation habits.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Human re-auditing of stratified samples of scored false positives from several top detectors will reclassify a substantial fraction as true objects, and correcting the ground truth will compress the precision spread among top models while leaving weaker models comparatively unaffected.
why_important: If top-model comparisons are annotation-noise comparisons, current leaderboard order among strong systems carries little information, and benchmark refresh with model-assisted exhaustive annotation becomes a priority.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Missing-annotation effects are known in principle, and a quantified saturation analysis showing top-of-leaderboard compression under corrected ground truth may be new for current model generations.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample scored false positives across models and confidence strata, obtain multi-annotator verdicts under the original guidelines, rebuild corrected ground truth for the audited subset, and recompute the model comparison.
main_risk: Auditors influenced by model predictions may over-accept plausible boxes, requiring audit designs with prediction-blind verification arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scored false positives are treated as model hallucinations, and precision differences as genuine capability differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: As models surpass the annotation's completeness, the evaluation increasingly measures the annotation, an inevitable crossover that the field has no monitoring mechanism to detect.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Audit one hundred high-confidence false positives of one top detector against the original annotation guidelines and report the reclassification rate.

one_line_idea: Annotation conventions drift within datasets: box tightness and part-inclusion practices vary across annotation batches, and detectors learn the average, producing systematic per-batch evaluation bias.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Large datasets are annotated over time by changing worker pools under evolving instructions and quality control, and dataset cards do not expose batch-level annotation provenance to users.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Measurable annotation-style drift exists within standard detection datasets, recoverable by clustering annotation geometry statistics, models trained on the full data learn a style average that mismatches every batch, and evaluation error correlates with the batch-style distance from the average, meaning part of measured localization error is style mismatch rather than model imprecision.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Unsupervised analysis of ground-truth geometry, tightness proxies, part-inclusion signatures, will reveal batch-like structure within datasets, and per-cluster evaluation of one model will show localization scores varying by cluster beyond sampling noise.
why_important: Style drift inflates apparent model error, contaminates cross-dataset comparisons, and suggests style-conditioned training or evaluation as a cheap accuracy recovery.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotator disagreement is studied on repeated annotations, and forensic recovery of latent batch-style structure inside standard detection datasets may be unattempted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract geometry-style features from ground truth, cluster annotations, validate cluster reality against any available provenance metadata, and measure model localization error stratified by cluster.
main_risk: Style clusters could confound with scene-type clusters, so scene-controlled analysis is required to isolate annotation style from content.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A dataset's annotations are treated as one consistent convention defined by its published guidelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instructions underdetermine pixel-level decisions, worker pools change, and quality control is sampled, so convention drift is the expected outcome of the production process, not an anomaly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute tightness-proxy distributions over annotation time or file ordering for one dataset and test for non-stationarity in one analysis session.

one_line_idea: Granularity-ambiguous aggregates drive outsized detection error: stacks, piles, and clusters annotated inconsistently as one-or-many account for a disproportionate share of both false positives and misses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real scenes contain aggregations, stacked plates, fruit piles, paper bundles, where the instance decomposition is genuinely ambiguous, and annotation guidelines resolve such cases inconsistently or not at all.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Instances belonging to ambiguous aggregates carry error rates several times the dataset average for strong detectors, the errors are dominated by decomposition mismatch rather than detection failure, and excluding or tolerance-scoring the aggregate stratum meaningfully changes both absolute scores and method rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Flagging aggregate-ambiguous regions on evaluation subsets will show error concentration in that stratum across all models, high between-model agreement in predictions there despite label disagreement, and ranking shifts under aggregate-tolerant scoring.
why_important: If a definitional stratum dominates residual error, model comparison is noise-ranked by aggregate-handling luck, and annotation standards for aggregates would improve benchmark validity more than model changes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Instance-definition ambiguity is acknowledged, and its quantified contribution to detection error budgets with ranking consequences may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate aggregate-ambiguity flags on evaluation samples, compute stratified error budgets for a model pool, and re-score under decomposition-tolerant matching that accepts any consistent instance decomposition.
main_risk: Tolerance scoring for decompositions is technically involved, needing careful definition of acceptable decompositions to avoid rewarding degenerate outputs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Every ground-truth instance is treated as an objectively correct unit that models should reproduce exactly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where one object ends and the next begins in a pile is partly a convention, and charging models for convention mismatches conflates perception failure with definitional disagreement.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Flag aggregates in a few hundred images, compute one detector's error rate inside versus outside the flagged regions, and compare in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: High-IoU evaluation operates beyond the human agreement floor: inter-annotator box IoU distributions show that strict-threshold metrics score models against noise, and noise-floor-normalized metrics change conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection metrics include strict IoU thresholds as a precision-of-localization probe, and every ground-truth box is one annotator's draw from a distribution of defensible boxes for that object.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The distribution of inter-annotator IoU varies strongly by object size, boundary clarity, and occlusion, strict-threshold metrics frequently demand agreement beyond the human floor for whole object strata, and normalizing thresholds by the measured local noise floor produces materially different model scores and method orderings in the precision regime.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Repeated annotation of stratified object samples will show human IoU floors below strict evaluation thresholds for identifiable strata, and noise-normalized re-scoring will compress precision-regime differences among top methods while re-ranking some.
why_important: Scoring beyond the measurement floor manufactures fictitious differences, and a noise-aware metric would realign the localization-precision race with actually measurable quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotator variance for boxes has been measured in pockets, and a stratified noise-floor map integrated into evaluation as threshold normalization may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect multi-annotator boxes over stratified samples, estimate stratum-wise IoU floors, define floor-normalized thresholds, and re-score a public model pool comparing conclusions.
main_risk: Multi-annotator collection is costly, and floor estimates depend on annotator quality, requiring expert-versus-crowd calibration arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Strict IoU thresholds are treated as objective probes of localization precision, applicable uniformly across objects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A metric cannot meaningfully resolve differences finer than the reproducibility of its ground truth, a basic measurement principle that uniform strict thresholds ignore.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Double-annotate a few hundred boxes across size strata and compare the human IoU distribution against the strict thresholds in use.

one_line_idea: Detectors out-localize their own training labels: model predictions are systematically closer to multi-annotator consensus than the single-annotator boxes they were trained and evaluated on, so evaluation penalizes models for being right.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training and evaluation use single-annotator boxes, learning theory predicts that models trained on noisy targets regress toward the conditional mean, and the conditional mean of defensible boxes may be more accurate than any single draw.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For well-trained detectors, predicted boxes lie closer to multi-annotator consensus geometry than the original single-annotator ground truth does, so a measurable fraction of scored localization error is actually the label's error, and evaluating against consensus would raise measured model quality and differentially re-rank methods by their denoising ability.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On objects with newly collected multi-annotator consensus boxes, strong detectors' predictions will show smaller distance to consensus than the original labels show to consensus, with the effect largest on blurry-boundary and occluded objects.
why_important: The result would invert the usual reading of localization error, part of it indicts the benchmark, and would justify consensus-based evaluation subsets for the precision regime.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-denoising by models is known for classification, and a geometric demonstration that detectors surpass their own box supervision may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect consensus boxes for stratified samples, compute label-to-consensus and prediction-to-consensus distances for several detectors, and test the ordering with occlusion and boundary-clarity stratification.
